title: Comment from Jay M
comment:
My name is Jay, MSN, RN, PHN. I am a licensed registered nurse in the State of California with over 15 years of clinical experience, including credentials as an LVN, ADN, and MSN. I currently serve as Director of Nursing for a Home Health agency where I oversee patient care protocols, clinical compliance, and evidence-based practice implementation for a medically complex patient population.

I write in strong support of the inclusion of the following seven bulk drug substances on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List: BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon. I respectfully urge the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) to recommend their addition to Category 1, thereby restoring lawful access to these compounds through licensed compounding pharmacies operating under valid prescriptions from qualified practitioners.

The FDA's 2023 decision to classify these peptides as Category 2 substances effectively removed them from the compounding toolkit without a formal rulemaking process that weighed clinical benefit against risk. Practitioners and patients who had established safe, efficacious protocols were abruptly cut off from access. The July 23–24, 2026 PCAC review is an opportunity to correct that outcome through a rigorous, transparent, and clinically informed process.

Critically, Category 1 placement does not circumvent patient safety, it routes access through a framework of physician oversight, individualized prescriptions, and licensed pharmacy preparation. This is precisely the model that Section 503A was designed to support: personalized medicine, prepared safely, under the supervision of a qualified practitioner.

My support for the inclusion of these peptides is not a call for unregulated access. To the contrary, placing these substances on the Category 1 list restores order and accountability to what is currently an uncontrolled landscape. When legitimate compounding access is eliminated, patients do not simply forgo treatment. They seek alternatives through unregulated channels. Restoring lawful, prescription-based access through licensed 503A pharmacies is the most effective patient safety measure available to the FDA.

As a nurse and healthcare administrator, I am acutely aware of the consequences of regulatory gaps. The patients I serve deserve access to emerging therapies through safe, supervised, and compliant pathways.

I respectfully urge the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee to recommend the formal inclusion of BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List. The clinical evidence base, patient need, and existing prescriber demand collectively support this determination. The FDA should conclude its rulemaking promptly following the PCAC's recommendation and restore these compounds to compliant, practitioner-supervised use.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment for the record.

Respectfully submitted,

title: Comment from Anonymous
comment:
SUBMISSION TO: FDA Public Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895
RE: July 23-24, 2026 PCAC Meeting -- Bulk Drug Substances for the 503A Bulks List
DATE: May 28, 2026

To the Members of the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee:

I am a licensed 503A compounding pharmacy director with advanced credentials in Medicinal Biochemistry and Pharmacy. I submit these comments in support of including BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon on the 503A Bulks List.

I. THE 2023 RESTRICTION CAUSED REAL HARM

When the FDA moved these peptides to Category 2 in 2023, patients did not stop seeking them. They shifted demand away from licensed, quality-controlled 503A pharmacies toward unregulated online sources, overseas gray-market suppliers, and research-chemical vendors with no accountability, no sterility testing, and no physician oversight. The restriction did not reduce patient exposure -- it redirected it to sources that cannot be regulated or monitored. That is the opposite of patient safety.

II. THE CLINICAL CASE IS SOUND

BPC-157: A synthetic pentadecapeptide with well-characterized mechanisms involving angiogenesis, nitric oxide modulation, and GI cytoprotection. Its nominated indication -- ulcerative colitis -- represents a serious unmet need for patients who have failed or cannot tolerate conventional biologics. The science supports evaluation, not categorical prohibition.

TB-500 (Thymosin Beta-4 Fragment): An endogenous peptide involved in actin sequestration, cellular migration, and tissue repair. Clinical use in wound healing and orthopedic injury recovery has been consistent with preclinical data. Properly compounded TB-500 under physician supervision has demonstrated positive outcomes with no documented serious adverse events in my patient population.

MOTS-c: A mitochondria-derived peptide with demonstrated activity in insulin sensitivity and skeletal muscle glucose uptake. Its nominated indications -- obesity and osteoporosis -- represent major public health burdens. Licensed compounding access would channel clinical use toward supervised, accountable settings.

Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon: Each has a legitimate scientific literature base supporting mechanism and clinical application. Prohibition of compliant compounding does not eliminate patient access -- it eliminates safe, supervised access.

III. QUALITY CONCERNS ARGUE FOR REGULATED COMPOUNDING, NOT PROHIBITION

The FDA cited immunogenicity risks, impurities, and insufficient human data. These concerns are valid -- and they are precisely why compounding through licensed 503A pharmacies operating under USP <797> sterile standards, with FDA-registered bulk suppliers, third-party finished-product testing, and patient-specific prescriptions, is the appropriate regulatory response. A licensed pharmacy provides accountability that no gray-market source can match.

IV. RECOMMENDED CONDITIONS FOR INCLUSION

1. Bulk substances sourced from FDA-registered suppliers with full Certificate of Analysis.
2. Independent third-party testing of finished preparations, documented in batch records.
3. Dispensing only pursuant to a valid patient-specific prescription with documented clinical rationale.
4. Adverse event tracking maintained by compounding pharmacies to build the evidence base.

These conditions are consistent with existing 503A standards. They represent responsible access, not unrestricted access.

V. CONCLUSION

Patients are already accessing these peptides. The only question is whether they access them through a licensed, regulated, accountable pharmacy -- or through an uncontrolled source. Inclusion on the 503A Bulks List answers that question in favor of patient safety.

I respectfully urge the Committee to recommend inclusion of all seven peptides under review on the 503A Bulks List.

Submitted by: A licensed 503A compounding pharmacy director

title: Comment from Daniel Goebel
comment:
I am submitting this comment in strong support of including KPV (lysine-proline-valine) on the 503A Bulks List for use in compounded preparations.
I am a patient who has spent the past two and a half years navigating a complex, multi-system inflammatory condition with features consistent with Mast Cell Activation Syndrome. My documented history includes elevated plasma histamine (3.4 ng/mL against a reference of ≤1.8), total IgE that nearly doubled from 525 to 900 IU/mL over one month, alopecia areata, chronic tendon and muscle tightness, exercise-induced rhinitis, and paresthesia. I have undergone bilateral open piriformis release and sciatic nerve decompression surgeries, completed 18 sessions of physical therapy, and trialed numerous medications including gabapentin, pregabalin, cyclobenzaprine, celecoxib, baricitinib (Olumiant), and multiple courses of corticosteroids, with minimal to no sustained improvement in my core symptoms.
After five days of oral KPV at 500 mcg twice daily, my chronic muscle and tendon tightness, refractory to every conventional treatment listed above, substantially resolved. This is the most significant clinical improvement I have experienced in over two years of active treatment across multiple specialty providers, including rheumatology, neurology, orthopedic surgery, pain management, and a comprehensive workup at Mayo Clinic.
KPV's mechanism as an anti-inflammatory and mast-cell-stabilizing tripeptide addresses a clinical need that is poorly served by existing FDA-approved therapies for mast cell and chronic inflammatory conditions. Currently approved options are limited, frequently ineffective for refractory patients, and often carry significant side effect burdens. For patients like myself who do not respond adequately to antihistamines, corticosteroids, or immunomodulators, access to compounded KPV through a licensed 503A pharmacy under physician supervision represents a meaningful therapeutic option.
Including KPV on the 503A Bulks List would allow patients to access this peptide through regulated compounding pharmacies with appropriate physician oversight, quality controls, and clinical monitoring, rather than forcing patients toward unregulated sources when conventional treatments fail. This is fundamentally a patient safety issue: the question is not whether patients will seek out KPV, but whether they will obtain it through a regulated pathway or an unregulated one.
I urge the FDA to include KPV on the 503A Bulks List to preserve access to this therapeutic option for patients with complex inflammatory and mast cell conditions who have exhausted standard-of-care treatments.

title: Comment from Nick Freidline
comment:
To the Food and Drug Administration,

I am writing on behalf of TruPeptide (trupeptide.co), an independent, non-commercial platform providing compound profiles, FDA status tracking, and consumer education on peptide therapies. We do not sell peptides or accept vendor payments.

1. Restricted access drove consumers to unregulated sources

When peptides were placed on the Category 2 list in 2023, demand did not decrease — it migrated to gray-market research chemical vendors with no physician oversight, inconsistent purity, and no adverse event reporting. Independent testing has repeatedly found gray-market peptide products to be mislabeled, underdosed, or contaminated. The Category 2 restriction did not reduce peptide use. It reduced the safety of peptide use.

HHS Secretary Kennedy stated on April 15, 2026: "This action begins to restore regulated access and will immediately begin shifting demand away from the black market." The question before this committee is whether the evidence supports formalizing that shift through the 503A bulks list.

2. The April 2026 removal was procedural — PCAC is the right venue

The removal of 12 peptides from Category 2 was triggered by withdrawal of the underlying nominations, not a substantive FDA safety determination. The July PCAC review is the appropriate venue for that evaluation, and we welcome it. Prolonged ambiguity benefits no one except unregulated suppliers.

3. Regulated infrastructure is already being built

In February 2025, Hims & Hers acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility in anticipation of regulated access. A positive PCAC recommendation would not create new demand — it would redirect existing demand from unregulated sources to regulated ones.

4. Requests to the committee

Publish evaluation criteria clearly so pharmacies and clinicians understand the basis for decisions.
Consider real-world alternatives: the relevant comparison is compounded peptide from a regulated pharmacy versus an unregulated overseas product with no quality controls.
For compounds where evidence is insufficient, specify what evidence would be needed — creating a pathway rather than a permanent exclusion.

title: Comment from Adam Thomas
comment:
Re: Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895 — Bulk Drug Substances for Section 503A Bulks List

I am a practicing physician submitting comments to provide clinical context on the potential role of several peptide-based bulk drug substances under consideration. My focus is on specific, limited indications where compounded formulations may address unmet needs in patients who have failed, cannot tolerate, or are not candidates for FDA-approved therapies.

BPC-157 (free base / acetate) — Ulcerative Colitis (UC)
Although evaluated for UC, there may be a subset of patients with refractory inflammatory disease who do not respond adequately to standard therapies (e.g., aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, biologics) or who experience significant adverse effects. In such cases, there is clinical interest in adjunctive therapies that may support mucosal healing. Compounded BPC-157 may be considered in highly selected patients under careful supervision when conventional options are exhausted or not tolerated.

KPV (free base / acetate) — Wound Healing and Inflammatory Conditions
KPV has potential anti-inflammatory effects that may be useful in localized applications. In practice, there is a need for non-steroidal options in patients who cannot tolerate corticosteroids or where systemic therapy is undesirable. Potential indications include chronic wounds, localized inflammatory conditions, and post-procedural healing. Compounded topical formulations may allow targeted therapy with minimal systemic exposure.

TB-500 (free base / acetate) — Wound Healing
Chronic, non-healing wounds (e.g., diabetic ulcers, post-surgical complications) remain a significant challenge. For patients who fail standard wound care, clinicians often have limited alternatives. TB-500 has been associated with tissue repair mechanisms, and compounded formulations may offer a potential adjunct in carefully selected, refractory cases.

MOTs-C (free base / acetate) — Obesity and Osteoporosis
In obesity management, some patients cannot tolerate or have contraindications to approved medications. Similarly, osteoporosis treatments may be limited by side effects or access issues. MOTs-C’s proposed metabolic effects suggest a possible role in patients who are not candidates for standard therapies, although use would be limited to carefully selected cases.

Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, Epitalon — Neurologic and Sleep Disorders
There remains a need for alternatives in conditions such as opioid withdrawal, refractory insomnia, migraine, and trigeminal neuralgia, particularly where existing treatments are ineffective or poorly tolerated. These agents may have potential roles in narrowly defined populations under physician oversight.

Conclusion
Across these substances, the most relevant use cases involve refractory patients requiring individualized therapy after standard treatments have failed or are not tolerated. Compounded formulations may provide flexibility in dosing and administration that is not otherwise available.

I encourage the Committee to consider inclusion of these substances for limited, clinically appropriate indications, recognizing the role of physician judgment, informed consent, and careful monitoring in their use.

I would be available to provide additional clinical perspective if helpful to the Committee.

Thank you for your consideration.

title: Comment from Christopher Bailey
comment:
I am writing in support of preserving a lawful, medically supervised compounding pathway for the peptide-related bulk drug substances currently under review, including BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide/DSIP, Semax, and Epitalon.

I understand that these substances raise legitimate questions about safety, quality, purity, appropriate use, and the limits of available clinical evidence. I am not asking FDA to ignore those concerns. I am asking FDA to address them through regulation, informed consent, and pharmacy quality standards rather than through restrictions that push patients into unregulated markets.

My position is grounded in my own experience. I have used peptides, and I have also had to navigate the gray market. I did not enter the gray market because I wanted to avoid medical supervision. I entered it because medically supervised access had become difficult, expensive, or unavailable. That distinction matters.

When patients lose access to compounded peptides through licensed pharmacies, many do not simply stop seeking them. They search online. They find vendors selling products labeled “for research use only” or “not for human consumption.” They compare dosing strategies in forums and private groups. They rely on anecdotal reports, incomplete information, and certificates of analysis of uncertain reliability. This is not a safer environment. It is a less visible one.

Restricting access does not eliminate demand. It often displaces demand into less regulated spaces.

A lawful compounding pathway gives patients, prescribers, and pharmacies a safer alternative, allowing individuals to seek compounds through a licensed clinician and compounding pharmacy rather than anonymous online suppliers. It supports sourcing, clearer labeling, informed consent, clinical monitoring, and adverse-event reporting.

For many, peptides represent an avenue of choice. People seek them for recovery from injury, support for inflammation, tissue repair, sleep, metabolic health, cognitive function, aging-related concerns, and overall quality of life. Clearly, not every claimed use is equally supported by evidence. Patient experience is not randomized clinical data. But patients often make medical decisions under uncertainty in consultation with clinicians after reviewing risks, benefits, alternatives, and unknowns. That same model should apply here.

Adults should be able to make informed choices about their own bodies when those choices are made with a prescriber and licensed pharmacy. A specific prescription, informed consent, and medical oversight should be sufficient for adults to access these compounds through regulated channels. Safeguards should be built into the pathway rather than used to eliminate the pathway.

Commercial pharmaceuticals may be unavailable, unaffordable, not covered by insurance, or not appropriate for a person’s specific needs. When access is limited only to branded products, a pharmaceutical paywall is created. That paywall determines who gets options and who does not.

Compounded therapies help dismantle that paywall. They provide more affordable, individualized options for people who otherwise may have no realistic avenue of access. Access and safety should not be treated as opposites. A well-regulated compounding pathway can advance both.

FDA should distinguish between irresponsible marketing and responsible patient-specific compounding. Misleading claims should be addressed. Products of unknown purity and sterility should not be promoted for human use. But licensed compounding pharmacies operating under appropriate standards are different. A patient-specific prescription written by a qualified clinician is different. A patient who has been informed of risks and uncertainties is different. The current environment creates a perverse incentive. Patients who want to be careful may have fewer lawful options than patients willing to take risks online. The system should reward responsible behavior by making the safer path easier to access than the unsafe path.

I respectfully urge FDA and the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee to support inclusion of the peptide-related bulk drug substances under review on the 503A Bulks List, subject to reasonable safeguards. Those safeguards should include prescription access, licensed compounding pharmacy preparation, appropriate sourcing and testing, clear labeling, informed consent, documentation of medical rationale, adverse-event monitoring, and restrictions on misleading marketing claims.

I am not asking FDA to pretend these compounds are risk-free. I am asking FDA to recognize that risk is better managed through lawful, supervised access than through prohibition or excessive restriction. Patients shouldn't be forced to choose between unaffordable pharmaceutical options and unregulated gray-market products. There should be a safer middle path. Licensed compounding pharmacies can provide that path.

Christopher Bailey
El Paso, Texas

title: Comment from Revia LLC
comment:
Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895
Submitted by: Michael Stone, Owner, Revia LLC, Fort Myers, FL. mss@revialife.com, June 10, 2026
Re: Support for Inclusion of BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-C, Semax, Epitalon, and Emideltide on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List
I am writing in support of the PCAC's review of the seven bulk drug substances nominated for inclusion on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List. I submit this comment as the owner of Revia LLC, a US-based supplier of research-grade peptides operating under a US 503(b) contract manufacturing relationship with full cGMP, ISO, and third-party testing documentation.
THE RESTRICTION CREATED THE PROBLEM IT WAS MEANT TO PREVENT.
When the FDA moved these compounds to Category 2 in 2023 and 2024, patient demand did not diminish — it relocated from licensed compounding pharmacies operating under USP 795/797 standards to an unregulated gray market of imported bulk API with no FDA oversight, no identity verification, no heavy metals testing, and no stability documentation. Independent testing of gray market peptide products has documented heavy metal contamination, purity failures, and identity mismatches. The restriction did not eliminate unsafe product. It eliminated the regulated alternative to it.
QUALITY-DOCUMENTED US SUPPLIERS ARE BEING TREATED IDENTICALLY TO BAD ACTORS.
Our operation sources exclusively from a US-registered 503(b) contract manufacturer. Every batch undergoes independent third-party testing: identity by LC-MS, purity by RP-HPLC, stability documentation, and heavy metals by ICP-MS — lead, arsenic, mercury, and cadmium. We maintain full certificates of analysis on every batch under cGMP and ISO standards.
Under the current framework, our operation is treated identically to a vendor importing untested bulk API from overseas with no documentation. Policy should distinguish between quality-documented suppliers and bad actors. A framework that sweeps both into the same enforcement category while failing to eliminate the gray market serves neither patient safety nor public health.
THE PATH FORWARD IS REGULATED ACCESS.
Adding these compounds to the 503A Bulks List creates a regulated pathway through which licensed compounding pharmacies — operating under prescription, USP standards, and state board oversight — can supply these compounds under physician supervision. That is precisely what the current situation lacks.
The compounds under review have accumulated meaningful research literature, years of supervised patient use prior to the 2023 restrictions, and a clinical safety record that does not support their Category 2 classification. Their administrative removal from Category 2 in April 2026 acknowledges as much.
I also urge the Committee to apply the same reasoning to the five compounds scheduled for February 2027 review — GHK-Cu, LL-37, Dihexa, PEG-MGF, and Melanotan II — and to expedite rulemaking for all twelve substances.
The regulated pathway is the safer pathway. The Committee has the opportunity to open it.
Respectfully submitted, Michael Stone, Owner, Revia LLC, June 10, 2026

title: Comment from westbrook daniel
comment:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am submitting this comment in support of maintaining responsible, physician-directed access to compounded peptide therapies through properly licensed pharmacies and qualified healthcare providers.

I understand and respect the FDA’s responsibility to protect the public from unsafe, contaminated, ineffective, or poor-quality products. Patient safety should always be the first priority. However, I also believe that eliminating or severely restricting access to certain peptide therapies through legitimate medical channels may unintentionally increase the very risks regulators are trying to prevent.

There is already substantial public demand for peptide therapies. When patients cannot access these therapies through licensed healthcare providers and regulated pharmacies, many do not simply stop seeking them. Instead, they often turn to the gray market, online research chemical websites, overseas suppliers, social media sellers, and other unverified sources.

That creates a serious public health concern.

Unregulated peptide products may be mislabeled, contaminated, improperly dosed, degraded, or manufactured without appropriate quality controls. Patients may receive products with unknown purity, unknown sterility, incorrect concentration, or no meaningful oversight. They may also use these products without medical screening, proper dosing guidance, lab monitoring, informed consent, or follow-up care.

In my opinion, the safer path is not to drive patients away from medical oversight. The safer path is to allow responsible access through trained medical providers and licensed pharmacies operating under appropriate federal and state standards.

When peptides are prescribed and monitored by qualified clinicians, patients can be evaluated properly. Providers can review health history, medications, contraindications, lab work, treatment goals, adverse effects, and clinical response. Pharmacies can be held to standards for sourcing, sterility, documentation, testing, labeling, storage, and patient instructions. This structure is far safer than forcing motivated patients into an unregulated market.

I support a regulatory framework that allows continued access to appropriate peptide therapies when there is a legitimate practitioner-patient relationship, pharmacy quality oversight, clear labeling, appropriate testing, and responsible clinical monitoring.

I also encourage FDA to consider a balanced approach that distinguishes between unsafe gray-market activity and legitimate pharmacy-compounded therapies provided under medical supervision. These are not the same thing. Restricting legitimate clinical access may unintentionally benefit the gray market and increase patient harm.

Patients deserve access to therapies through the safest possible pathway. For many peptide therapies, that pathway should be through licensed healthcare providers and qualified pharmacies, not anonymous online sellers.

I respectfully urge FDA and the Advisory Committee to consider the real-world consequences of limiting access. A practical, quality-focused framework for physician-directed and pharmacy-dispensed peptide therapy would help protect patients, reduce gray-market use, improve oversight, and support responsible medical care.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment.

Respectfully,

Daniel Westbrook

Denying the inclusion of these peptides on the 503(B) bulk substances list will not stop consumer utilization; it will simply relegate it to dangerous, subterranean markets. By allowing qualified 503(B) facilities to compound these peptides, the FDA can successfully bring this therapeutic avenue into the light—ensuring standardization, transparency, and clinical oversight.

title: Comment from Eichorn Wesley
comment:
Public Comment Supporting Inclusion of BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide(DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon on the 503A Bulks List

To the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee and FDA Review Staff:

I am a licensed physician writing in support of adding BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide(DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon to the 503A Bulks List. My perspective is grounded in clinical experience and in the medical ethics principles of beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, and respect for patient autonomy.

Patients are already seeking and using these substances. When regulated access is unavailable or unclear, some patients obtain them from less reputable sources, including internet vendors and research-chemical suppliers. In those settings, identity, purity, dose accuracy, sterility, storage conditions, and contamination risk may be unknown. In my view, this creates a preventable safety problem.

From the standpoint of beneficence, I believe these substances have meaningful potential for benefit in carefully selected patients under medical supervision. Patients are seeking options for conditions involving gastrointestinal dysfunction, inflammation, tissue repair, sleep, neurologic symptoms, metabolic concerns, and other chronic health issues where conventional options may be limited, poorly tolerated, or unaffordable. I recognize that additional research is needed and that inclusion on the 503A Bulks List would not make these substances FDA-approved drugs. However, the presence of uncertainty should not automatically force patients into unregulated channels.

I also have personal experience relevant to this issue. As a physician, I made the informed decision to take oral BPC-157 and noticed a clear improvement in gut health that was directly correlated in time with its use. I do not present this as definitive proof of efficacy, but I do believe such clinical and personal observations are relevant when considered alongside biologic plausibility, patient-reported outcomes, and the need for safer access pathways.

From the standpoint of nonmaleficence, regulated compounding access would likely reduce harm compared with the current gray-market environment. A 503A pathway would allow licensed prescribers and legitimate pharmacies to provide clearer sourcing, quality standards, dosing consistency, documentation, informed consent, monitoring for benefit, and monitoring for adverse effects. Excluding these substances from regulated compounding does not necessarily protect patients; it may simply leave them to obtain peptides without medical guidance or reliable quality oversight.

From the standpoint of justice, access and affordability should be considered. Some patients cannot afford or tolerate very expensive conventional medications. Others have limited options despite ongoing symptoms. Compounded peptides may offer a more accessible alternative for selected patients when used responsibly. Justice does not require that every therapy be available without limits, but it does support creating a safe, regulated pathway rather than leaving access only to those who can navigate costly or unregulated sources.

From the standpoint of autonomy, competent adults should be able to make informed medical decisions in partnership with licensed clinicians. We allow adults to make many choices involving known risk such as alcohol use despite substantial evidence of harm. By contrast, these peptides, when obtained through regulated compounding pharmacies and used under physician supervision, may offer potential benefit within a more controlled and transparent risk environment. Respecting autonomy does not mean ignoring safety; it means supporting informed choice in the safest feasible setting.

I respectfully recommend that the Committee and FDA add BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide(DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon to the 503A Bulks List. Inclusion would not represent FDA approval or proof of efficacy. Rather, it would create a more responsible pathway for clinician-supervised use, reduce reliance on questionable sources, improve safety monitoring, and preserve appropriate medical judgment.

For these reasons, I support inclusion of these substances on the 503A Bulks List.

Respectfully submitted,
Wesley Eichorn, DO

title: Comment from M. M.
comment:
Re: Docket FDA-2025-N-6895

I am a board-certified family medicine and lifestyle medicine physician who incorporates preventive medicine, obesity medicine, and hormone replacement therapy into my practice. I am writing in support of maintaining rigorous FDA oversight of compounded peptide products and encouraging a regulatory framework that prioritizes patient safety and high-quality clinical evidence.

Compounding has an important and well-established role in healthcare when it serves individual patient needs that cannot be met by commercially available FDA-approved medications. However, I am concerned that an increasing number of novel peptide products are being marketed and prescribed outside of this traditional role, often in the rapidly expanding wellness and longevity industry.

For many of these peptides, there remains limited high-quality evidence regarding efficacy, optimal dosing, pharmacokinetics, long-term safety, immunogenicity, reproductive effects, and clinically meaningful outcomes. While preliminary laboratory or animal data may be promising, these findings should not be viewed as substitutes for well-designed human clinical trials.

My concern is not that peptide research should be discouraged. On the contrary, I strongly support continued investigation into these compounds. However, widespread clinical use should follow—not precede—the generation of adequate safety and efficacy data.

Patients frequently assume that a compounded prescription carries the same level of evidence and regulatory review as an FDA-approved medication. This misunderstanding can create unrealistic expectations and expose patients to therapies whose benefits and risks have not been adequately characterized.

In addition, the rapid commercialization of these products within largely cash-pay wellness practices creates financial incentives that may outpace the available scientific evidence. A robust regulatory framework helps ensure that clinical adoption is driven by demonstrated patient benefit rather than market demand.

Importantly, stronger FDA oversight does not hinder innovation. Rather, it creates incentives for sponsors to conduct the rigorous clinical trials necessary to establish safety and effectiveness. This process ultimately benefits patients by producing standardized manufacturing, reliable quality control, evidence-based prescribing, and the possibility of broader access through conventional healthcare channels and insurance coverage.

I respectfully encourage the FDA to continue applying rigorous scientific standards when evaluating peptides proposed for compounding and to reserve widespread clinical availability for products supported by sufficient evidence of safety, quality, and efficacy.

As a clinician, I would welcome the availability of safe and effective peptide therapies supported by robust clinical evidence. Strong FDA oversight is not an obstacle to that goal—it is the pathway that gives physicians and patients confidence that these therapies truly provide more benefit than harm.

Thank you for your consideration and for your continued commitment to protecting public health.

title: Comment from Locascio Nick
comment:
I am a 32-year-old male patient, and I am writing in strong support of adding BPC-157 and KPV to the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List. These peptides helped me reverse a serious autoimmune and immune-dysregulation picture, and I have used them under physician supervision with laboratory testing before and after. I want to tell you exactly how they fit the uses you are evaluating — and why the way I am currently forced to obtain them is the real danger here.
Where I started. For years I carried an interlocking set of conditions that fed one another: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis with markedly elevated thyroid antibodies, chronic Epstein-Barr virus reactivation, and the immune dysregulation driving both. On top of that sat a fatigue I could not out-train, out-sleep, or out-diet — I have an athletic build and disciplined habits, and I was still exhausted. My stool testing showed significant dysbiosis with pathogenic bacterial overgrowth. And one food after another was turning into an allergy: egg, gluten, walnut, beef, and more each showed elevated food-specific IgE on testing and provoked real reactions when I ate them. The list of foods I could safely eat kept shrinking. This is the real-world profile of gut and immune dysregulation these peptides are used to treat, and I lived inside it.
BPC-157 — nominated for ulcerative colitis. I don’t have ulcerative colitis. But BPC-157 is nominated for the repair of inflamed, dysregulated gut tissue, and that is precisely what I used it for and precisely where it worked. On BPC-157, my gut markers moved from a high-risk range into a healthy one on repeat testing, the pathogenic overgrowth cleared, and the GI symptoms that had disrupted my days resolved. And as my gut healed, my food allergies healed with it. Beef is the clearest case: I was allergic to beef — it flagged on every panel and I had cut it out of my diet completely — and after this protocol my beef antibodies dropped back to normal and I now eat beef with no reaction at all. That allergy is simply gone, and it is not the only food I have won back. BPC-157 targeted exactly the process at issue in this nomination, and it delivered.
KPV — nominated for wound healing and inflammatory conditions. KPV is a potent anti-inflammatory peptide, and it is the “inflammatory conditions” use you are reviewing that it served for me. Used alongside BPC-157, it helped bring a genuinely dysregulated immune system back into balance. As that picture normalized, the chronic fatigue that had shadowed me for years lifted. I function today at a level I had started to believe was gone for good.
Now the part that should concern this Committee. Every time I use one of these peptides, I am afraid. Because they are not available through a regulated pharmacy, I have had to buy them from unregulated “research use only” suppliers — vials with no guarantee of identity, purity, sterility, or potency, made by someone I cannot verify and tested by no one. Every dose, I weigh a real risk of injecting a contaminated or mislabeled product against the real benefit these peptides bring to my health. No patient should have to make that calculation. There should be a better way — and there already is one. It is called compounding.
That is what this listing does. Adding BPC-157 and KPV to the 503A list does not create a new risk; it eliminates one that exists right now. It replaces the anonymous gray-market vial with a valid prescription, a licensed compounding pharmacist, USP-grade ingredients, verified sterility and potency, and physician oversight with lab monitoring. That is the standard of care I want and cannot legally get. The current policy has not stopped patients like me from using these peptides — it has only guaranteed that we use them at the greatest possible risk.
My request. Recommend the inclusion of BPC-157 and KPV on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, and give patients a safe, prescription-based, professionally supervised pathway to therapies that are already changing our lives.

title: Comment from Rachdi Younès
comment:
The very purpose of 503A is to provide a pathway for substances without a USP monograph or FDA-approved application. Requiring NDA-level evidence would render the list meaningless. The relevant standard is whether these substances can be compounded safely under pharmacy oversight, not whether they have proven efficacy for a specific indication.
The argument that names and salt forms (e.g., acetate vs. free base) are not standardized is actually an argument in favor of inclusion, not against it. Adding these substances to the list would impose clear specifications, forcing suppliers to comply with official standards. Keeping them off the list perpetuates exactly the confusion the FDA seeks to avoid.
Current policy has not eliminated patient demand. It has simply driven patients into unregulated gray-market channels: online retailers, medical spas, and "research use only" suppliers. In these channels, there are no guarantees of purity, sterility, accurate dosing, or proper storage. This is a far greater health risk than a compounded preparation made in a licensed pharmacy under cGMP.
Adding these peptides to the 503A list would enhance safety.
Inclusion would ensure:

· Traceable sourcing from qualified API manufacturers.
· Mandatory purity, potency, and sterility testing.
· Clear labeling and dosing guidance.
· Adverse event reporting through official pharmacovigilance channels.
These peptides have favorable safety profiles.
Animal studies and accumulated clinical experience with BPC-157, TB-500, and Epitalon show minimal toxicity and generally mild adverse effects. The rare serious events cited (cardiac, melanoma) are not specifically attributable to these peptides. More importantly, pharmacy-controlled compounding would drastically reduce risks related to impurities or contamination.

title: Comment from Blanton Corey
comment:
Re: Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895
Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee; Bulk Drug Substances Nominated for Inclusion on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List

I submit this comment in my personal capacity as a patient, veteran, and registered nurse, and not on behalf of any employer, pharmacy, manufacturer, or trade organization. I am writing as a veteran, registered nurse, and patient to support continued patient and physician access to safe, regulated compounded peptides through licensed clinicians and properly regulated compounding pharmacies.

For years, my experience in the conventional medical system — particularly within VA care — felt less like health care and more like sick care. I was not being optimized. I was being managed. Problems were addressed only after they became serious enough to treat, useful therapies were started and stopped, and my care was largely reactive. During that time, my physical health, weight, energy, strength, mood, and overall function were as poor as they had been in years.

Beginning around September 2025, with a more proactive and individualized approach that included compounded peptide therapy as part of a broader health plan, my health changed dramatically. I am not describing a theory or a marketing claim. I am describing my lived clinical trajectory.

I went from approximately 270 pounds to 214 pounds by March 2026. My blood pressure improved. My strength improved. My energy, mood, body composition, recovery, and daily function improved. My objective data — including weight, vital signs, lab trends, and functional performance — moved in the same direction as my subjective experience. For me, this was the difference between being medically maintained and actually becoming healthy again.

Compounded peptides were not a magic bullet, and I am not asking FDA to ignore safety concerns. I fully understand that compounded medications are not the same as FDA-approved drugs. I also understand that purity, sterility, potency, route of administration, aggregation, impurities, labeling, and patient monitoring matter. As a nurse, I take those concerns seriously.

But the answer to safety concerns should be regulation, quality standards, pharmacist oversight, physician judgment, and patient-specific prescriptions — not policies that drive patients into the gray market.

If safe, regulated access is restricted too broadly, many patients will not simply stop seeking these therapies. They will be pushed toward unregulated websites, research-chemical sellers, offshore suppliers, unknown powders, questionable certificates of analysis, and products with no meaningful clinical oversight. That outcome does not protect patients. It increases risk.

Licensed compounding pharmacies, accredited facilities, physicians, pharmacists, and appropriate quality-control standards provide a safer path than prohibition. The policy choice should not be “unrestricted peptide access” versus “no access.” The better question is whether patients and clinicians will have a lawful, regulated, transparent pathway — or whether patients will be forced into an unregulated market because legitimate access has been made too expensive, too narrow, or practically impossible.

Peptides have been part of a genuine health turnaround in my life. I went from a state that felt like managed decline to a state of substantially improved health, supported by both subjective improvement and objective markers. Patients with chronic conditions, veterans, and people who have already been failed by reactive care models should not lose access to individualized therapies when those therapies are prescribed and monitored responsibly.

I respectfully ask the Committee and FDA to preserve access to safe, regulated compounded peptides where appropriate under Section 503A. FDA should distinguish between unsafe gray-market peptide sales and legitimate compounding by licensed pharmacies for identified patients under clinician supervision. Stronger standards, better documentation, adverse-event reporting, source verification, potency testing, sterility testing, and patient monitoring are reasonable. Eliminating practical access is not.

Please keep the regulated pathway open. Patients deserve safety, but we also deserve access, medical judgment, and the opportunity to pursue optimal health rather than merely being managed in decline.

The FDA’s July 23 agenda includes BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, and MOTS-c; July 24 includes Emideltide/DSIP, Semax, and Epitalon. also recognizes that 503A compounding depends on specific bulk-substance requirements, including USP/NF status, FDA-approved components, or inclusion on the 503A bulks list.

title: Comment from Rogers Michael
comment:
To the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee,

I am submitting this comment regarding Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895 and the review of BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, emideltide/DSIP, Semax, and Epitalon/Epithalon for potential inclusion on the 503A Bulks List.

I strongly support regulated, physician-supervised access to these peptides.

My position is based on both public health and personal autonomy. Competent adults should have broad freedom to make informed decisions about their own bodies, especially when working with licensed medical professionals. The federal government should not default to restricting access simply because a compound is new, politically controversial, commercially disruptive, or not yet fully developed through the traditional pharmaceutical approval pathway.

I recognize that these peptides are not FDA-approved drugs for the proposed uses. I also recognize that the available evidence varies, and that many wellness-market claims are ahead of the science. But those facts do not justify forcing patients into an unregulated gray market.

The FDA should distinguish between two very different realities:

One reality is unregulated online sales, unknown purity, unknown dosing, unknown sterility, and no medical oversight.

The other reality is physician-supervised care through licensed compounding pharmacies using quality-tested bulk substances, clear documentation, patient-specific prescriptions, and informed consent.

These should not be treated as equivalent.

If the FDA is concerned about safety, the answer should be higher standards, not prohibition. If the FDA is concerned about poor-quality products, the answer should be identity testing, purity testing, potency verification, sterility requirements, endotoxin limits, and traceable certificates of analysis. If the FDA is concerned about exaggerated marketing, the answer should be enforcement against false claims, not denying access to patients and physicians who are trying to act responsibly.

A regulated 503A pathway could include:

Verified identity and purity of bulk substances

Potency and amount-per-vial testing

Sterility and endotoxin standards where appropriate

Required certificates of analysis

Physician supervision

Patient-specific prescriptions

Informed consent documents

Clear disclosure that the compounds are not FDA-approved for the proposed use

Adverse event reporting

Restrictions against misleading commercial claims

That type of framework would protect patients better than simply removing physician-supervised options.

A blanket rejection would not end peptide use. It would push more people toward gray-market suppliers, overseas vendors, and products with no meaningful quality control. That is a predictable harm. If the FDA’s goal is public safety, it should prefer regulated access over unregulated demand.

I also believe the committee should be honest about the economic incentives involved. Restricting compounded access often benefits large pharmaceutical companies by reducing competition from lower-cost pharmacy-based alternatives. That may not be the stated purpose of regulation, but it is often the practical effect. The public has reason to be skeptical when safety arguments consistently lead to outcomes that protect large incumbent manufacturers while limiting patient choice and physician discretion.

The FDA should protect the public from unsafe products and fraudulent claims. It should not protect pharmaceutical monopolies from competition.

title: Comment from Tyler Wiseman
comment:
I am writing to support patient and physician access to safe, regulated compounded peptides.

Don’t Ban the Medicine — Regulate It.

The case for keeping therapeutic peptides legal, tested, and above board.

Every medicine we trust today was once unproven. Insulin was experimental. Penicillin was experimental. So was tesamorelin — a peptide, prescribed in clinics across this country right now, because someone was once allowed to study it. Hold onto that word. Allowed.

Let’s be precise about what we’re actually debating, because precision is where bad policy goes to die. No one is asking to hand out unlabeled vials on street corners. And despite the headlines, “peptides” are not some uniform contraband — the word covers insulin, FDA-approved drugs, and a mystery powder bought off an anonymous website, all at once. The question was never “peptides: yes or no.” It is where we draw the line, and whom we trust to draw it.

Here is the line the government drew. A few years ago, the FDA moved more than a dozen peptides into a restricted category that told licensed compounding pharmacies, in plain effect: you may no longer make these for your patients. The stated reason was safety — too little human data, real questions about how the immune system responds to injected peptides. Those concerns are not fabricated. I will be the first to say so.

But watch what actually happened next. The demand did not vanish. It moved. When you bolt the regulated door, you do not close the market — you hand it to whoever is waiting in the alley behind the building. A patient who once received a tested preparation from a pharmacy — sourced from a registered facility, with a certificate of analysis, under a physician’s supervision — now types a few words into a search bar and wires money to a stranger overseas for a powder of unknown purity, unknown dose, unknown everything.
So ask yourself, honestly: which of those two people is safer? Prohibition did not remove the risk from the equation. It removed the oversight. It kept the danger and threw away the safeguards.

This builds a trap with no exit. The agency says these compounds lack rigorous human data. Fair enough. But how is rigorous human data ever created? Through supervised medical use and through clinical trials — both of which require a lawful on-ramp. So the logic collapses into a closed loop: we can’t permit it, because there’s no evidence — and you can’t build the evidence, because we won’t permit it. That is not caution. That is a locked room where science quietly suffocates.

Now put faces on this, because policy is never abstract to the people living inside it.
Think of a veteran with a shoulder that never fully healed, who finally found relief under a doctor’s care — and now watches that option disappear, nudged toward the gray market, or toward nothing at all.

Think of the physician — a careful one, a good one — forced to practice in a fog where a therapy that is defensible today may be a violation in six months; who must choose between abandoning a patient and risking a license. We should be angry that we put healers in that position.

Think of the researcher holding a molecule that might genuinely help people, with no legal path to prove it — watching promising science stall not for lack of merit, but for lack of a door.
I am not asking you to believe peptides are magic. They are not. Some will prove useless. Some carry real risks, and contamination in the unregulated market has already hurt people — and that is exactly my point. You do not fix a purity problem by driving patients to the least pure supply on earth. You do not fix a data problem by outlawing the only road to data.

So here is the ask. Not deregulation — stewardship. Keep a clear, published list of what may be compounded. Demand pharmaceutical-grade sourcing, certificates of analysis, genuine quality control. Punish fraud and false miracle-cure marketing without mercy. And fund an honest, expedited path to the trials that will finally tell us what works and what doesn’t.

Even the nation’s top health officials now make a version of this argument — that blanket restrictions created a black market, and that the remedy is regulated access, not prohibition. On that, they are right.

A ban feels like safety. It is not. It is a blindfold we tie over our own eyes and call it protection. I would rather we keep our eyes open — regulate the medicine, test it in daylight, and let evidence, not fear, decide what stays.

This is Tyler Wiseman and you for considering my comment.

title: Comment from A. J. Jimenez
comment:
To Whom It May Concern:

My name is AJ, and I am a United States Marine Corps veteran submitting this comment in support of reinstating several research peptides—including BPC‑157, TB‑500, MOTS‑C, Semax, and KPV—to the FDA’s compounding list. I am providing this statement as a patient, a veteran, and a citizen who has directly experienced the consequences of their removal.

I respectfully urge the FDA to consider the substantial number of Americans who were already receiving these peptides through licensed clinicians before the 2023–2024 regulatory changes. When these compounds were removed from the compounding list, thousands of patients—including myself—were forced into a grey‑market environment. This shift did not eliminate demand; it eliminated medical oversight. Patients who previously relied on physician guidance were suddenly left without legal access to therapies that had been improving their quality of life. Many individuals, including veterans with complex medical histories, were left to research protocols, safety considerations, and product verification on their own. Some of us have the background and discipline to do this responsibly; many do not.

As a Marine veteran, I underwent multiple reconstructive surgeries on both ankles and a knee during active duty, along with other service‑connected disabilities. Years of chronic pain, limited mobility, and mental fatigue left me severely overweight and depressed. After re‑injuring one of my reconstructed ankles, I was told that fusion was the only remaining option. With no other medical alternatives offered, I began researching peptides independently.

BPC‑157 and TB‑500 were instrumental in my recovery. These compounds supported my joint comfort, mobility, and tissue resilience to a degree that allowed me to begin exercising again. That progress led to meaningful weight loss, improved physical function, and a return to a lifestyle that resembles the active Marine I once was. I am now in my early forties, but before beginning this path, I felt physically and mentally decades older.

For cognitive clarity, mitochondrial resilience, and mood stabilization, I incorporated MOTS‑C, Semax, and Emideltide. These compounds helped me regain focus, energy, and a sense of vitality that had been diminished after years of chronic pain and what I believe may have been toxic exposures during military service. While I understand that these peptides are still under investigation, the improvements I have experienced are significant and life‑changing.

My wife, an Air Force veteran, has also benefited. After years of severe gastrointestinal issues and endometriosis culminating in a hysterectomy, she continued to struggle despite repeated medical visits. The only solutions offered were pain medications, fiber supplements, and dietary changes—none of which improved her condition. After beginning KPV, TB‑500, and BPC‑157, she reported meaningful relief within six weeks. For the first time in years, she feels hopeful.

We are not isolated cases. Many patients—veterans, chronic‑pain sufferers, individuals with inflammatory conditions, and those with limited conventional treatment options—have reported similar experiences. Public forums, patient communities, and clinician networks contain thousands of accounts describing improved mobility, reduced inflammation, enhanced recovery, and better quality of life. While anecdotal evidence is not a substitute for clinical trials, it is a signal that should not be ignored.

Preclinical research on these peptides is extensive. These findings do not claim definitive human outcomes, but they do demonstrate biological plausibility and justify continued supervised clinical use rather than forcing patients into unregulated markets.

The FDA’s mission includes protecting public health. In this case, removing access has unintentionally increased risk. Reinstating these peptides to the compounding list—under appropriate quality, purity, and oversight standards—would restore safe, physician‑guided access and reduce the harm caused by grey‑market sourcing.

I respectfully request that the FDA consider the lived experiences of veterans like myself, the needs of patients who have exhausted conventional options, and the substantial preclinical evidence supporting further supervised use. These compounds have materially improved my life, my wife’s life, and the lives of many others. We ask that you restore legal, medically supervised access so patients can pursue these therapies safely and responsibly.

Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,
AJ
United States Marine

title: Comment from Brian Danusis
comment:
Dear FDA Commissioner and Review Committee:

I am writing as a private citizen and hopeful future peptide user to express my support for creating a clear regulatory pathway that allows safe, legal, and appropriately supervised access to therapeutic peptides.

I appreciate and support the FDA's mission to protect public health by ensuring that medical products are safe, effective, and manufactured according to rigorous quality standards. At the same time, I believe the current regulatory environment surrounding many peptides has created significant challenges for patients seeking legitimate access to potentially beneficial therapies.

My interest in peptides arose from my efforts to address ongoing health and recovery challenges. As a 50-year-old person with an active lifestyle that includes BJJ, golf, and weightlifting, medial epicondylitis has significantly impacted my ability to enjoy these activities and has diminished my quality of life. I have most recently tried PRP Therapy in conjunction with physical therapy, with no real notable improvement.

As someone who has explored the possibility of using peptides, I am concerned about the limited availability of products through regulated channels and force individuals toward unregulated or "grey market" sources, where product quality, purity, sterility, dosing accuracy, and manufacturing practices may be uncertain. Restricting access without providing a practical and lawful pathway does not eliminate demand; rather, it may increase the likelihood that consumers obtain products from sources that lack appropriate oversight.

I respectfully encourage the FDA to consider policies that:

Promote Safe and Legal Access - Establish clear regulatory pathways for peptides with reasonable evidence of safety and therapeutic potential. Encourage legitimate development and commercialization through FDA-regulated channels.

Prioritize Quality and Manufacturing Standards - Require robust Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards. Ensure products are tested for identity, purity, potency, and sterility. Increase transparency regarding manufacturing and quality assurance.

Support Physician-Guided Use - Allow qualified healthcare professionals to evaluate whether peptide therapies are appropriate for individual patients. Encourage informed consent and evidence-based decision making between patients and providers.

Facilitate Research and Data Collection - Expand opportunities for clinical investigation of peptides that show promise in areas such as tissue healing, metabolic health, age-related conditions, and other therapeutic applications. Use real-world evidence and post-market surveillance to further inform regulatory decisions.

Reduce Reliance on Unregulated Markets - Recognize that patient demand exists regardless of regulatory restrictions. Create a framework that incentivizes consumers to obtain products through legitimate, regulated channels rather than from unverified online suppliers.

I believe the FDA can best protect public health by balancing safety concerns with practical access. Patients should not be forced to choose between foregoing potentially beneficial therapies and purchasing products from unregulated sources of uncertain quality. A well-defined regulatory framework can support both patient safety and medical innovation.

Thank you for considering my comments and for your continued efforts to protect and improve public health. I respectfully urge the FDA to pursue policies that expand safe, regulated, and evidence-based access to peptide therapies while maintaining the high standards that patients and healthcare professionals expect.

Sincerely,
Brian Danusis
Coventry, Rhode Island

title: Comment from Rachdi Younès
comment:
The very purpose of 503A is to provide a pathway for substances without a USP monograph or FDA-approved application. Requiring NDA-level evidence would render the list meaningless. The relevant standard is whether these substances can be compounded safely under pharmacy oversight, not whether they have proven efficacy for a specific indication.
The argument that names and salt forms (e.g., acetate vs. free base) are not standardized is actually an argument in favor of inclusion, not against it. Adding these substances to the list would impose clear specifications, forcing suppliers to comply with official standards. Keeping them off the list perpetuates exactly the confusion the FDA seeks to avoid.
Current policy has not eliminated patient demand. It has simply driven patients into unregulated gray-market channels: online retailers, medical spas, and "research use only" suppliers. In these channels, there are no guarantees of purity, sterility, accurate dosing, or proper storage. This is a far greater health risk than a compounded preparation made in a licensed pharmacy under cGMP.
Adding these peptides to the 503A list would enhance safety.
Inclusion would ensure:

· Traceable sourcing from qualified API manufacturers.
· Mandatory purity, potency, and sterility testing.
· Clear labeling and dosing guidance.
· Adverse event reporting through official pharmacovigilance channels.
These peptides have favorable safety profiles.
Animal studies and accumulated clinical experience with BPC-157, TB-500, and Epitalon show minimal toxicity and generally mild adverse effects. The rare serious events cited (cardiac, melanoma) are not specifically attributable to these peptides. More importantly, pharmacy-controlled compounding would drastically reduce risks related to impurities or contamination.

title: Comment from Robert King
comment:
Re: Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895 — 503A Bulk Drug Substances; Peptide Access

I am writing as a practicing physician in support of a lawful, physician-supervised pathway for patient access to the peptide substances under review: BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, emideltide/DSIP, Semax, and Epitalon-related bulk drug substances.

This is not a request for therapeutic adventurism or internet “anti-aging” commerce. It is a request for regulatory prudence. Patients are already seeking these agents. If legitimate access is extinguished, use will not disappear; it will migrate to foreign suppliers, “research use only” vendors, unverified gray-market vials, uncertain sterility, uncertain potency, uncertain endotoxin burden, and self-directed dosing without physician supervision or adverse-event reporting.

FDA’s own meeting materials identify serious evaluated uses: BPC-157 for ulcerative colitis; KPV for wound healing and inflammatory conditions; TB-500 for wound healing; MOTS-c for obesity and osteoporosis; emideltide/DSIP and Epitalon-related substances for sleep disorders; and Semax for cerebral ischemia, migraine, and trigeminal neuralgia. These are not trivial wellness endpoints. They are chronic, recurrent, disabling, and expensive conditions that drive office visits, emergency visits, hospitalizations, procedures, specialty care, impaired function, and public-payer expense.

The economic context is sobering. CMS reported about $5.3 trillion in U.S. national health expenditures in 2024, including $1.118 trillion in Medicare spending and $931.7 billion in Medicaid spending. Chronic wounds affect an estimated 8.2 million Medicare beneficiaries and have been associated with Medicare costs of roughly $28.1 to $96.8 billion annually. Obesity accounts for nearly $173 billion in annual U.S. medical expenditures. Stroke-related costs are approximately $56.2 billion annually. Osteoporotic fractures among Medicare beneficiaries have been estimated to cost about $57 billion annually. Chronic insomnia also imposes large direct and indirect costs through impaired function, accidents, comorbidity, and lost productivity.

These figures do not prove that any single peptide will solve these problems. But they do show the magnitude of the public-health opportunity if even modest gains can be achieved in wound healing, inflammatory disease activity, obesity-related morbidity, osteoporosis-related fracture risk, chronic insomnia, migraine burden, trigeminal neuralgia, or post-ischemic neurologic disability. A responsible access pathway could allow careful use while generating the data needed to separate promising therapies from ineffective ones.

The safety issue should be framed candidly. No bioactive compound is risk-free. FDA has legitimate concerns about immunogenicity, aggregation, peptide impurities, API characterization, sterility, endotoxin exposure, route of administration, and limited human data. But these concerns argue for standards, not prohibition. Patients are safer when products are compounded by qualified pharmacies using registered bulk-substance manufacturers, valid certificates of analysis, identity testing, potency testing, sterility testing, endotoxin testing, impurity specifications, lot traceability, clear labeling, and physician oversight. They are less safe when regulation forces demand into opaque markets beyond meaningful scrutiny.

I therefore urge FDA to support inclusion of these nominated peptide bulk substances on the 503A bulks list, or at minimum to establish a conditional access framework requiring licensed prescriber involvement, documented medical rationale, informed consent, clear disclosure that compounded products are not FDA-approved drugs, restrictions on exaggerated marketing claims, lot-level traceability, and mandatory adverse-event and outcome reporting.

This approach would preserve access for patients with difficult chronic conditions, reduce reliance on unregulated supply chains, encourage higher manufacturing and pharmacy standards, and create real-world safety and outcome data for future regulatory decisions.

A categorical ban may appear cautious, but in practice it may be the more dangerous course. It would not protect patients from peptides; it would protect unregulated sellers from scrutiny. Patients deserve neither credulous enthusiasm nor bureaucratic indifference. They deserve the protection of physician judgment, pharmacy standards, transparent quality controls, honest labeling, pharmacovigilance, and disciplined evidence development.

For these reasons, I respectfully ask FDA and the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee to support regulated, physician-supervised access to these peptide substances through the 503A framework, with safeguards robust enough to protect patients while preserving therapeutic innovation and the possibility of meaningful Medicare and Medicaid savings.

title: Comment from Brian Murphy
comment:
I am a student at George Washington University with a strong interest in exercise science and nutrition, and a genuine passion for training and the gym. I am writing to share a perspective in support of preserving access to BPC-157 and related peptides being considered for the 503A Bulks List.
What has shaped my view most is what I have seen firsthand among people I know. Several friends of mine dealing with stubborn soft-tissue and tendon injuries were recommended BPC-157 by their own physicians, who directed them to third-party compounding suppliers because no conventional option was helping them heal. In these cases the results were striking: injuries that had lingered for months improved rapidly, and these individuals were able to return to training and normal activity far sooner than expected. For active people, the difference between a nagging injury that never fully resolves and one that heals is enormous, both physically and mentally.
I want to be candid that I understand the science here is still maturing. The long-term clinical research in humans is limited, and that is a legitimate concern the Committee should weigh carefully. But the answer to incomplete evidence should be more research and responsible oversight, not cutting off access to a substance that patients and their doctors are already finding genuinely effective. When physicians themselves are recommending a therapy because it works where others have failed, that real-world signal deserves serious consideration.
I respectfully urge the Committee to support keeping BPC-157 accessible through legitimate compounding channels while encouraging the rigorous long-term studies that will let its benefits and risks be fully understood. Thank you for considering public input on this important issue.

title: Comment from Mario Marcolongo
comment:
The Committee should recommend that BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon be added to the Section 503A Bulks List, against FDA staff's current proposal to exclude all seven.
Furthermore, the reasoning below outlines a foundational risk-evaluation framework that should serve as the default standard for maximizing risk reduction and real-world data acquisition over preemptive administrative restriction.

The relevant regulatory principle is not complicated: restrictions on what a person does with their own body are justified when the action harms someone else, not merely when it carries personal risk. Antibiotic resistance is the clean example of the first kind, the damage compounds and lands on people who never made the choice. Nothing in this docket resembles that. Whatever risk these seven substances carry is absorbed by the person who accepted it, under a prescription and a pharmacist's oversight.

The obvious objection is that personal risk becomes a public cost the moment it reaches an emergency room. The U.S. already prices that kind of risk through insurance and personal liability for every other legal risk activity, from motorcycling to elective surgery, rather than prohibiting it. There's no reason to treat compounded peptides differently.

There's also a positive case for this, not just a permissive one. People already using these compounds outside formal trials are, in effect, an existing population of real-world exposure data, exactly what FDA's own four-factor test for this list already asks about, since "historical use of the substance in compounded drug products" is one of its four criteria, and exactly the kind of evidence FDA's own Real-World Evidence framework, built under Section 3022 of the 21st Century Cures Act, exists to use. This matters more here than for a typical drug: these are cheap, easily synthesized peptides with little commercial incentive behind a traditional trial program, so compounded, prescription-based use isn't a supplement to that evidence pathway, for several of them it's effectively the only one that will ever exist. None of it is usable if the product is an anonymous vial with unknown dose and provenance. A 503A prescription is documented and traceable by design. Excluding these substances doesn't just increase individual risk. It deletes a population's worth of evidence along with it.

If part of the concern is marketing rather than the molecules themselves, that's a different problem with an already-functioning fix. FDA issued more than fifty warning letters in September 2025 over exactly this kind of misleading marketing and mislabeled "research use only" sales, using its existing misbranding and advertising authority, a mechanism aimed at the claims and the people making them, not at the substance itself. It doesn't require removing 503A access for prescribers who make no such claims, and it keeps working whether or not these seven substances stay on the list. If anything, closing the legitimate channel leaves the marketing-driven, unregulated side of this market with less competition, not less to sell.

If the concern is impurity or inconsistent synthesis, which FDA's own briefing materials do raise, the fix is tighter oversight of the raw-material supply chain, ideally reshored to FDA-registered API manufacturers, not eliminating the one channel where a pharmacist is accountable for what's in the product. The gray market these substances get pushed into has none of FDA's four criteria available to evaluate, and generates no data anyone can use going forward.

The Committee should reject FDA staff's proposal to exclude all seven substances and instead recommend their inclusion on the 503A Bulks List, paired with stronger sourcing standards for raw material suppliers.

title: Comment from Martell Eric
comment:
Compounded medications and peptide therapies play a critical role in personalized medicine by providing treatment options for patients whose needs cannot be met by commercially available products. Many patients require customized dosing, alternative formulations, allergen-free preparations, or medications that are otherwise unavailable due to shortages or discontinuation. Compounding pharmacies help bridge these gaps, ensuring continuity of care and improving patient outcomes. In specialties such as hormone replacement therapy, weight management, chronic disease management, and regenerative medicine, compounded therapies allow healthcare providers to tailor treatment plans to individual patient needs, promoting greater adherence, tolerability, and therapeutic success.

Peptide therapies represent an emerging area of medicine with significant potential to improve patient health, quality of life, and preventive care outcomes. Under the supervision of licensed healthcare providers, peptides are being utilized to support metabolic health, recovery, tissue repair, hormone optimization, and overall wellness. Restricting access to these therapies could limit innovation and reduce treatment options for patients who have not achieved satisfactory results with traditional therapies. Rather than imposing broad limitations, regulatory efforts should focus on maintaining rigorous quality standards, transparency, and patient safety while preserving access to safe, physician-directed compounded medications and peptide therapies. Such an approach supports both public health and the advancement of personalized, evidence-informed medical care.

Eric Martell, MSN, APRN, FNP-C

title: Comment from Anonymous
comment:
I appreciate the opportunity to provide public comment regarding the FDA's consideration of peptides such as BPC-157.

As a board-certified nurse practitioner who has incorporated peptide therapy into clinical practice, I understand the importance of evidence-based medicine and the FDA's responsibility to protect public safety. While it is true that BPC-157 lacks the large, randomized controlled trials that many approved therapies have, I respectfully ask the Agency to also consider the substantial body of real-world clinical experience accumulated by licensed healthcare providers.

Over more than three years of practice, I prescribed compounded injectable BPC-157 to hundreds of appropriately selected patients, most commonly at doses of 250-750 mcg daily for approximately 12-week courses, once or twice per year as clinically indicated. During that time, I observed consistently positive outcomes, particularly for tendon and ligament recovery, musculoskeletal healing, gastrointestinal symptoms, and reduction of inflammation. Equally important, I observed very few side effects and no serious adverse events attributable to the medication.

While anecdotal experience should not replace rigorous clinical trials, it should not be dismissed entirely. Real-world evidence has historically played an important role in identifying both therapeutic benefit and safety signals, and the collective experience of clinicians who have responsibly prescribed these therapies deserves consideration alongside the current published literature.

My greatest concern is that restricting legal access will not eliminate demand. Patients who believe BPC-157 has benefited them will likely turn to unregulated online vendors selling products labeled as "research use only." These products are not dispensed under the supervision of licensed healthcare professionals, may not meet the same quality standards as regulated U.S. compounding pharmacies, and are more likely to expose patients to contamination, inaccurate dosing, or counterfeit ingredients.

Allowing licensed providers to prescribe BPC-157 through appropriately regulated U.S. compounding pharmacies offers a safer alternative than driving patients toward the grey market. It preserves physician oversight, informed consent, appropriate patient selection, dosing guidance, monitoring for adverse effects, and quality-controlled manufacturing.

I respectfully ask the FDA to consider maintaining a legal pathway for qualified healthcare providers to prescribe compounded BPC-157 while additional clinical research continues. Patient safety is best served not only by evaluating available evidence, but also by ensuring patients have access to regulated products under the care of licensed medical professionals rather than forcing them into unregulated channels.

Thank you for your consideration and for your commitment to protecting public health.

title: Comment from Powers Randy
