**Subject: Public Comment on Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895 – Strong Support for Inclusion of BPC-157 on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List**

**Submitted via regulations.gov**
**Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895**
**Submitted by: Randy Powers, R.Ph.**
**Powers Family Pharmacy**
**2315 Technology Drive, O’Fallon, MO 63368**
**Date: June 18, 2026**

Dear Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee Members and FDA Reviewers,

I am writing to provide public comment in strong support of including **BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate** on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List.

I am a compounding pharmacist with **25 years of experience** at Powers Family Pharmacy in O’Fallon, Missouri. We specialize in customized, patient-specific formulations prepared in full compliance with USP <795> and <800> standards. However, I am currently **prevented from compounding BPC-157** for patients due to its present classification and status outside the 503A Bulks List. This restriction limits our ability to meet legitimate medical needs for patients who could benefit from this substance.

Several years ago, I personally sustained a significant soft tissue injury while working out. The injury resulted in persistent pain, swelling, and limited mobility that affected both daily activities and my training. After appropriate research, I used BPC-157 and experienced **great relief** from the pain and inflammation. The improvement in healing and return to normal function was noticeable and meaningful. This personal experience reinforced what I have observed in patient reports regarding BPC-157’s potential benefits for tissue repair and recovery.

In my professional practice, I have seen patients with musculoskeletal injuries, slow-healing wounds, and certain inflammatory conditions who could benefit from compounded BPC-157 preparations when conventional therapies fall short. Adding BPC-157 to the 503A Bulks List would allow licensed compounding pharmacies to provide these customized formulations under appropriate regulatory oversight and quality standards.

I respectfully urge the Committee to recommend the inclusion of BPC-157 (free base and acetate) on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List. This step would restore access for patients who need it while maintaining the safety and quality framework that compounding pharmacies already follow.

Thank you for considering my comments and for your important work on this issue. I am available to provide additional information if requested and can be reached at **636-265-2924** or **randy@powerscompounding.com**.

Sincerely,

**Randy Powers, R.Ph.**
Compounding Pharmacist

title: Comment from Ahmad Myra
comment:
I am submitting this comment as a healthcare entrepreneur with direct experience building patient-facing care infrastructure at scale. My background is in medicine and the science underlying these compounds, and my work over the past several years has been in designing systems that connect patients to providers and compounding pharmacies across a wide range of therapeutic categories. I write in support of including BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide, Semax, and Epitalon on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List.

Leading a company that has served more than half a million patients has taught me one consistent lesson. When patients need something the system doesn't offer, they don't stop needing it. They find it somewhere else. The demand for these peptide therapies is real, it is growing, and it does not disappear when a regulated pathway is unavailable. What changes is where patients go to meet it.

When compliant 503A pharmacies cannot legally compound these substances, patients turn to grey market online vendors, international suppliers, and unregulated sources with no quality controls, no pharmacy oversight, and no clinical accountability. I have seen this pattern directly. The regulatory gap does not suppress use. It redirects it toward less safe options, and the patients absorbing that risk are often the most medically vulnerable: people managing chronic inflammatory conditions, sleep disorders, cognitive decline, and metabolic disease for whom conventional pharmaceuticals have provided incomplete relief.

There is also a structural problem for operators trying to build legitimate care pathways. Without a clear 503A Bulks List designation, healthcare platforms and the providers practicing on them face real legal and operational uncertainty around whether compounding relationships can be structured in a compliant way. A regulated pathway enables compliant operators to build with confidence. Regulatory ambiguity pushes patients and providers toward less accountable alternatives.

I also want to note the cost and access implications. Compounded peptides, when available through licensed 503A pharmacies, are substantially more affordable for patients than comparable branded options. For patients managing chronic conditions on constrained budgets, access to compounded therapies is not a convenience. It is often the difference between continuing care and abandoning it. These downstream health consequences rarely surface in regulatory proceedings, but they are real.

My recommendation is that the Committee support inclusion of all seven substances under review. The patients who need these therapies are already seeking them. The question before the Committee is whether they will be able to access them through a regulated, quality-controlled pathway, or whether they will continue to be pushed outside the system that could protect them.

I appreciate the Committee's time and consideration, and I am grateful for the opportunity to contribute to this process.

Myra Ahmad, MD

title: Comment from Pulsipher Kari

To Whom It May Concern,

I am a Registered Nurse practicing in Utah and respectfully submit this comment in support of preserving access to provider-prescribed compounded peptides from FDA-regulated 503A compounding pharmacies.

Every day, I care for patients who are looking for evidence-based options to improve their health, quality of life, and overall wellness. For some patients, compounded peptide therapies prescribed by licensed healthcare providers offer individualized treatment options when commercially available medications do not meet their unique clinical needs.

Compounded medications prepared by licensed 503A pharmacies play an important role in patient care by allowing prescribers to tailor treatment based on medical necessity, dosage requirements, allergies, sensitivities, or other individualized considerations. Removing access to these therapies would significantly limit a healthcare provider's ability to develop personalized treatment plans for patients.

As healthcare professionals, we understand the importance of patient safety. We support appropriate oversight, high-quality manufacturing standards, transparent labeling, and evidence-based prescribing practices. However, eliminating access to compounded peptides through qualified 503A pharmacies would unintentionally reduce treatment options for many patients who are currently benefiting from physician-supervised care.

Patients deserve access to individualized therapies when prescribed by licensed medical professionals and compounded by pharmacies operating under applicable federal and state regulations. Rather than restricting access, I encourage the FDA to continue supporting strong quality standards while preserving the ability of healthcare providers to exercise clinical judgment in determining the most appropriate treatment for their patients.

Thank you for your consideration and for your continued commitment to protecting public health while ensuring patients maintain access to medically appropriate, individualized care.

title: Comment from Hadley Erica
comment:
To Whom It May Concern,
I am submitting this comment as a board-certified Family Nurse Practitioner and Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetist who provides evidence-based, patient-centered care in a rural community. I strongly support continued patient access to regulated compounded peptides prescribed by licensed healthcare providers and prepared by accredited compounding pharmacies.
In my practice, I care for patients who often have limited access to specialty care and who are looking for additional options to improve their health, function, and quality of life. While peptides are not a substitute for good nutrition, exercise, sleep, or evidence-based medical care, they can serve as valuable adjuncts in carefully selected patients when used within a comprehensive treatment plan.
My patients receiving peptide therapy are evaluated through a complete medical history, physical examination, informed consent process, ongoing laboratory monitoring when appropriate, and routine follow-up visits. They are educated on potential risks, expected benefits, adverse effects, and the limitations of current evidence. These therapies are not provided casually or without oversight. They are prescribed within an established provider-patient relationship with continued monitoring and accountability.
One of my greatest concerns is that restricting access to regulated compounded peptides will not eliminate patient demand. Instead, it will drive many patients toward unregulated online vendors and black-market sources that lack quality assurance, sterility testing, potency verification, and medical oversight. As healthcare providers, we routinely care for patients who have already purchased medications from unreliable internet sources because they were unable to obtain appropriate treatment through legitimate medical channels. Restricting access through licensed providers is likely to worsen this problem rather than improve patient safety.
Accredited compounding pharmacies operate under established quality standards and are subject to regulatory oversight. Prescriptions written by licensed healthcare professionals create an additional layer of safety through individualized patient evaluation, documentation, informed consent, and ongoing monitoring. This regulated pathway provides significantly greater protection for patients than forcing them into an unregulated marketplace.
As a clinician, I believe regulatory efforts should focus on improving product quality, pharmacy oversight, transparency, adverse event reporting, and provider education rather than broadly limiting access to compounded peptides for appropriately selected patients.
Every therapy in medicine requires thoughtful consideration of risks and benefits. Peptides should be held to appropriate standards of safety and quality, but patients should continue to have access to therapies that may improve healing, recovery, metabolic health, body composition, and overall quality of life when prescribed responsibly by qualified healthcare professionals.
I respectfully urge the FDA to preserve access to regulated compounded peptides through licensed providers and accredited compounding pharmacies while continuing to strengthen oversight that protects patients. This balanced approach promotes both patient safety and patient autonomy while reducing the likelihood that individuals will seek potentially unsafe products from unregulated sources.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments.
Erica Hadley, MS, CRNA, FNP-C
Backroads Beauty Aesthetics
Burlington, Kansas

I respectfully ask the Committee to carefully consider the impact that restricting access to compounded peptides would have on patients and healthcare providers.

title: Comment from Klucznik Shaun
comment:
**Public Comment in Support of Adding the Listed Peptide-Related Bulk Drug Substances to the 503A Bulks List**

I respectfully submit this comment in support of allowing continued physician-directed and pharmacist-compounded access to BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide, Epitalon, and Semax, including both free base and acetate forms where applicable. FDA’s own briefing materials identify these substances as under consideration for the 503A Bulks List and explain that the agency uses a balancing test that considers chemical characterization, safety issues, effectiveness evidence, and historical use. That framework supports a measured regulatory approach rather than categorical exclusion.

I oppose FDA’s proposal not to include these substances on the 503A Bulks List. The better approach is to permit access through regulated compounding while requiring clear identity standards, Certificates of Analysis, sterility and endotoxin testing for injectable products, impurity and aggregation testing, appropriate labeling, physician oversight, and adverse-event reporting. Prohibiting lawful compounding does not eliminate demand. It risks pushing patients toward unregulated foreign, gray-market, or research-chemical sources where quality controls, patient counseling, and medical supervision are weaker.

FDA’s concerns appear to center largely on incomplete data, inconsistent naming conventions, lack of certain public characterization data, and limited clinical evidence. Those are real concerns, but they are not the same as a finding that these substances are categorically unsafe or should be removed from supervised medical access. For example, FDA notes concerns with BPC-157 characterization and limited clinical safety data, but also acknowledges limited human rectal-enema studies in which no serious adverse events were reported, while noting the data were limited. The appropriate response to incomplete data is tighter quality standards and better reporting, not removal of access.

For KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Epitalon, Emideltide, and Semax, FDA similarly identifies data gaps, potential immunogenicity concerns, or lack of human data. Those issues can be addressed through risk-based compounding controls, especially for injectable routes. FDA’s own documents repeatedly identify peptide aggregation, impurities, endotoxin testing, and route of administration as central concerns. Those are manufacturing, testing, labeling, and monitoring issues. They are not, by themselves, sufficient grounds to remove all access through licensed pharmacies and licensed prescribers.

The existence of FDA-approved alternatives should not be treated as a reason to block individualized compounding. Approved therapies may not work for every patient, may cause intolerable side effects, may be unaffordable, or may not match a patient’s specific clinical circumstances. Section 503A exists because Congress recognized that individualized patient care sometimes requires compounding outside the standard approved-drug pathway. If FDA treats the mere existence of approved alternatives as a reason to exclude every nominated substance, the practical value of 503A access is substantially narrowed.

A regulated-access model would better protect the public. FDA could recommend that any permitted compounding require: verified chemical identity for the specific free base or acetate form; sourcing only from registered establishments; batch-specific Certificates of Analysis; sterility, endotoxin, impurity, and aggregation testing where applicable; route-specific labeling; informed-consent language explaining that the product is compounded and not FDA-approved; and mandatory adverse-event reporting. This would address the concerns FDA identified while preserving patient and physician choice.

I therefore urge FDA and the PCAC to recommend inclusion of BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide, Epitalon, and Semax-related bulk drug substances on the 503A Bulks List. At minimum, FDA should defer any negative determination and consider a conditional or risk-based pathway rather than a categorical prohibition. The most protective public-health approach is not to force these substances out of regulated compounding, but to keep them within a supervised, documented, quality-controlled framework.

title: Comment from Anonymous
comment:
Public Comment in Strong Support of Including BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, GHK-Cu, DSIP, Epitalon, MOTS-c, Semax, and Related Peptides on the 503A Bulks List (Docket FDA-2025-N-6895)

Dear Members of the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee and FDA Staff,

I am writing anonymously as a practicing healthcare provider with a doctorate and a master's degree, and I have performed clinical research and authored several studies published on PubMed. I have treated thousands of patients over my career and am well-respected in my field. I submit this comment to protect my professional reputation while sharing evidence-based observations from direct clinical experience. I strongly support the inclusion of BPC-157 (free base/acetate), TB-500 (free base/acetate), KPV (free base/acetate), GHK-Cu, DSIP, Epithalon, MOTS-c, Semax, and related peptides on the Section 503A Bulks List. These compounds deserve careful consideration for compounding access under appropriate oversight.

Personal and Clinical Experience
For over 20 years, I have lived with chronic issues stemming from joint surgery. I faced significant pain and limited function, and I believed another surgery was inevitable. After incorporating BPC-157 and TB-500, recovery improved dramatically, and surgery became unnecessary. Adding KPV, TB-500, BPC-157, and GHK-Cu produced even better results—the joint now feels the best it has in years with significantly fewer problems.

Beyond the joint, these and additional peptides have delivered broad systemic benefits. DSIP and Epitalon have significantly improved my sleep quality. MOTS-c has enhanced my running endurance and overall energy levels, eliminating the afternoon energy slump I once experienced. Semax provides superior focus, motivation, and productivity compared to caffeine, without the jitteriness. Collectively, my energy is markedly higher, and I feel approximately 10 years younger. These outcomes align with the peptides’ mechanisms supporting tissue repair, gut healing, inflammation modulation, mitochondrial function, neuroprotection, and cytoprotection.

In my practice, I have observed similar benefits in patients and friends struggling with chronic inflammation, injuries, recovery challenges, sleep issues, fatigue, and cognitive demands. These peptides offer targeted healing that addresses root causes rather than merely masking symptoms.

Broader Public Health Context
While these peptides face scrutiny, many substances with far greater risks remain widely approved and consumed: artificial food dyes linked to behavioral issues, excessive added sugars driving obesity and metabolic disease, and glyphosate (widely used in agriculture) with ongoing debates about long-term health impacts. Our population grows sicker and heavier despite (or partly because of) these exposures. Chronic inflammation contributes heavily to the leading causes of death—heart disease, cancer, stroke, and others—and drives enormous sick-care costs.

Peptides like BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, and others show strong potential to heal the gut barrier, reduce systemic inflammation, improve metabolic and mitochondrial function, and support recovery. They could meaningfully lower the national burden of chronic disease when used responsibly by licensed providers. Supporting safe, regulated access aligns with goals to “make America healthy again” by prioritizing genuine healing over perpetual symptom management.

Recommendations
I urge the Committee to recommend these peptides for the 503A Bulks List. This would enable:

More rigorous research under controlled conditions.
Safe sourcing and quality through regulated compounding pharmacies with proper testing, stability, and sterility standards—reducing risks from unregulated markets.
Expanded patient care options for licensed providers, with appropriate monitoring.

Patients and providers deserve access to tools that promote real healing, not barriers that push people toward less safe alternatives. I have seen the difference these peptides make firsthand. Denying regulated access does not eliminate demand—it risks safety and innovation.

Thank you for considering this comment. I welcome further dialogue through official channels and strongly encourage expanded research and a framework for safe patient access.

Respectfully,
A Concerned Healthcare Provider

title: Comment from Benjamin Spradlin
comment:
Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895
Subject: In Support of Adding BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Emideltide, Semax, and Epitalon to the 503A Bulk Substances List
Submitting As: Individual

To the Members of the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee,

I am writing as an individual citizen to urge the committee to vote in favor of adding BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon to the 503A Bulk Substances List. Excluding these compounds from legitimate compounding pharmacies does not eliminate public demand; instead, it creates a dangerous public health crisis by forcing patients into unregulated, overseas black markets.

My Personal Experience with Peptide Therapy I have personally experienced the life-altering benefits of the peptides currently under your consideration. For years, debilitating chronic pain dominated my daily existence and entirely prevented me from engaging in any meaningful exercise or physical activity. Incorporating these molecules into my care plan completely transformed my trajectory. By targeted reduction of my pain, these therapies allowed me to reclaim an active lifestyle, resulting in a profound and remarkable restoration of my overall quality of life. My experience is not unique; it represents the millions of Americans who rely on these therapies to function and thrive.

As the committee deliberates, I respectfully ask you to consider the following three critical pillars of public safety and clinical care:

1. Harm Reduction and Public Safety
Millions of Americans currently use these peptides for legitimate therapeutic reasons, including chronic wound healing, tissue repair, and metabolic support. If the FDA bans licensed compounding pharmacies from manufacturing these substances, the demand will not vanish. Patients will be forced to purchase these compounds from unregulated "research chemical" websites and foreign black markets. These illicit sources lack quality control, sterility testing, and professional oversight. By approving these peptides for the 503A list, the FDA brings these substances into the light—ensuring they are synthesized under strict cGMP guidelines, tested for purity, and dispensed under the supervision of qualified U.S. clinicians.

2. Preserving the Clinical Innovation of Compounding
The historical and statutory purpose of pharmacy compounding is to provide customized therapeutic solutions when standard mass-market pharmaceuticals fall short. Many patients suffering from severe, treatment-resistant conditions—such as refractory ulcerative colitis, chronic non-healing wounds, and severe nerve pain—have exhausted conventional, FDA-approved drugs. Compounded peptides offer a vital alternative pathway for personalized medicine. Denying access strips physicians of innovative tools required to treat complex patients who have found no relief elsewhere.

3. Real-World Evidence and Clinical Utility
While large-scale, multi-million-dollar randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are rare for non-patented, compounded substances, a vast body of real-world clinical data and peer-reviewed translational research demonstrates the safety and efficacy of these compounds. Peptides like BPC-157 and KPV possess well-documented anti-inflammatory and tissue-regenerative mechanisms. The lack of standard pharmaceutical sponsorship should not be mistaken for a lack of clinical utility.

Conclusion
A vote to restrict these seven peptides is a vote that inadvertently fuels an underground, unregulated marketplace, placing American consumers at risk. A vote to approve them protects public health by establishing a safe, regulated, and transparent framework for patient access. I strongly urge the committee to vote to add these peptides to the 503A Bulk Substances List.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and dedication to public health.
Sincerely, Benjamin Spradlin
San Antonio, Texas

title: Comment from Boyles James
comment:
I respectfully urge the committee to preserve a safe, regulated pathway for physician-directed access to compounded peptides when appropriate.

I fully recognize and support the FDA's responsibility to protect the public from unsafe, contaminated, or improperly manufactured products. High standards for quality, sterility, accurate labeling, and oversight are essential. Patient safety should remain the foundation of any regulatory framework.

At the same time, I encourage the committee to carefully consider the real-world consequences of restricting access without ensuring that practical, affordable alternatives are available. When legitimate avenues of care become unavailable, patients do not simply stop seeking treatment. title: Comment from Lear Kayla
comment:
Docket No. FDA-2026-N-2979
Re: Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting, July 23–24, 2026 — bulk drug substances nominated for the Section 503A Bulks List

To the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee and FDA staff:

I am submitting this comment as someone who works directly in the compounded medication space, supporting independent medical practices and providers who prescribe peptide therapies as part of individualized patient care. I work with a licensed 503A/503B pharmacy and see firsthand how patients access these medications when the system is working correctly: through a prescribing provider, a documented clinical need, and a pharmacy operating under real oversight– USP compounding standards, state board of pharmacy licensure, and FDA registration where applicable.

I urge the Committee to recommend inclusion of BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon on the Section 503A Bulks List.

Why this matters to the patients and providers I work with:
These peptides were removed from legal compounding access in 2023 without, in the experience of the clinicians I support, a specific safety signal that justified blanket restriction for every one of them. In the years since, I have watched what actually happens when regulated access disappears: patients don't stop seeking these therapies. They turn to unregulated "research chemical" vendors, gray-market importers, and unverified online sellers — sources with no sterility assurance, no potency verification, no adverse event reporting, and no prescribing oversight at all. That is a worse outcome for patient safety than the one the 2023 restriction was meant to prevent.

Licensed 503A pharmacies operate under meaningful accountability: batch testing, USP 795/797 sterile and non-sterile compounding standards, state board inspections, and a prescriber who has evaluated the patient and is monitoring the outcome. That infrastructure is the actual safeguard here — not the absence of access, but the presence of oversight. When regulated pathways narrow, they don't reduce demand; they just remove the safety layer between the patient and the product.

My request to the Committee:
Please weigh the evidence with this reality in mind: a "no" recommendation does not mean patients go without these therapies. It means they go without a pharmacist, a quality-controlled product, and a provider who can adjust treatment based on real clinical response. I've seen the difference that oversight makes for patient safety, and I ask the Committee to support continued, regulated access to these compounded peptides through licensed 503A pharmacies.

Thank you for your consideration.

title: Comment from Dover Shane
comment:
I am submitting this comment in support of adding the nominated bulk drug substances — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon — to the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List.

Favorable benefit-to-risk profile. These substances have accumulated years of clinical and practitioner use, with an adverse event record that is modest relative to the therapeutic interest they have generated. None of the nominated substances carry the toxicity, abuse potential, or narrow therapeutic index that typically justifies exclusion from compounding. Where risks exist, they are manageable through the same quality and oversight mechanisms Section 503A already requires — a licensed pharmacist or physician, a valid certificate of analysis, and manufacture by an FDA-registered facility. Categorical exclusion is a poor tool for managing a modest risk profile when tailored safeguards already exist.

Patient access and autonomy. Section 503A compounding exists precisely to serve patients whose needs are not met by commercially available, FDA-approved products — including individualized dosing, discontinued formulations, and emerging therapeutic uses not yet supported by an approved drug application. Patients and their prescribing physicians, not a categorical exclusion, are best positioned to weigh the individualized risks and benefits of a given therapy. Denying these substances a path onto the 503A list does not eliminate demand; it pushes patients toward unregulated, unverified sourcing outside any pharmacist or physician oversight, which is a materially worse outcome for patient safety than regulated compounding.

Consistent with FDA’s protective mandate. FDA’s role is to protect public health, which includes ensuring that patients who seek these substances can obtain them through a supply chain with quality controls, professional oversight, and accountability — the exact framework Section 503A provides. Inclusion on the Bulks List advances FDA’s protective mission by bringing these substances inside the regulated system rather than leaving them in an unregulated gray market. I urge the Committee to recommend, and FDA to finalize, inclusion of these substances on the Section 503A Bulks List.

Very Respectfully,
Shane Dover

title: Comment from Anonymous
comment:
I appreciate the opportunity to provide public comment regarding the FDA's consideration of peptides such as BPC-157.

As a board-certified nurse practitioner who has incorporated peptide therapy into clinical practice, I understand the importance of evidence-based medicine and the FDA's responsibility to protect public safety. While it is true that BPC-157 lacks the large, randomized controlled trials that many approved therapies have, I respectfully ask the Agency to also consider the substantial body of real-world clinical experience accumulated by licensed healthcare providers.

Over more than three years of practice, I prescribed compounded injectable BPC-157 to hundreds of appropriately selected patients, most commonly at doses of 250-750 mcg daily for approximately 12-week courses, once or twice per year as clinically indicated. During that time, I observed consistently positive outcomes, particularly for tendon and ligament recovery, musculoskeletal healing, gastrointestinal symptoms, and reduction of inflammation. Equally important, I observed very few side effects and no serious adverse events attributable to the medication.

While anecdotal experience should not replace rigorous clinical trials, it should not be dismissed entirely. Real-world evidence has historically played an important role in identifying both therapeutic benefit and safety signals, and the collective experience of clinicians who have responsibly prescribed these therapies deserves consideration alongside the current published literature.

My greatest concern is that restricting legal access will not eliminate demand. Patients who believe BPC-157 has benefited them will likely turn to unregulated online vendors selling products labeled as "research use only." These products are not dispensed under the supervision of licensed healthcare professionals, may not meet the same quality standards as regulated U.S. compounding pharmacies, and are more likely to expose patients to contamination, inaccurate dosing, or counterfeit ingredients.

Allowing licensed providers to prescribe BPC-157 through appropriately regulated U.S. compounding pharmacies offers a safer alternative than driving patients toward the grey market. It preserves physician oversight, informed consent, appropriate patient selection, dosing guidance, monitoring for adverse effects, and quality-controlled manufacturing.

I respectfully ask the FDA to consider maintaining a legal pathway for qualified healthcare providers to prescribe compounded BPC-157 while additional clinical research continues. Patient safety is best served not only by evaluating available evidence, but also by ensuring patients have access to regulated products under the care of licensed medical professionals rather than forcing them into unregulated channels.

Thank you for your consideration and for your commitment to protecting public health.

title: Comment from Hunt Dan
comment:
PCAC Public Comment — Docket FDA-2025-N-6895
Submitted by: Dan Hunt, Founder — Field Vitality (Maui, HI)

Chairman and Members of the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee,

I submit this comment as a healthcare entrepreneur who has spent the past year building a physician-led telehealth platform on Maui, Hawaii. I have witnessed firsthand the profound demand for peptide therapeutics and the consequences of restricting access to them.

Peptides are not experimental novelties. They are biologically fundamental signaling molecules that our bodies naturally produce. BPC-157 accelerates tissue repair in ways no conventional pharmaceutical matches. MOTS-C regulates mitochondrial function and metabolic health. TB-500 supports connective tissue recovery. These compounds have been used safely by thousands of patients under physician supervision for years.

The current regulatory gray zone — where peptides are neither fully restricted nor affirmatively authorized for compounding — does not protect patients. It drives them to unregulated sources. Every week in my community, I meet people who have turned to gray market peptide suppliers because they cannot access these therapies through legal channels. They buy unverified products from unregulated sources because the legitimate path is blocked.

Removing these peptides from Category 2 and placing them on the 503A Bulks List would:
- Bring patients back into regulated, physician-supervised care
- Enable licensed compounding pharmacies to produce quality-controlled products
- Reduce the gray market that currently thrives on regulatory uncertainty
- Allow telehealth platforms like ours to provide safe, monitored access

The evidence is clear. The demand is real. The patients are waiting.

I urge the committee to recommend removal of BPC-157, TB-500, MOTS-C, and the remaining peptides from Category 2 restrictions and affirm their place on the 503A Bulks List for compounding.

Respectfully,
Dan Hunt
Founder — Field Vitality
Maui, HI

title: Comment from Creech Jared
comment:
Committee Members —

I urge you to vote against measures that would effectively block 503A compounding pharmacies from preparing the listed peptides.

- BPC-157 (Reviewed primarily for ulcerative colitis)
- TB-500 (Reviewed primarily for wound healing)
- KPV (Reviewed for inflammatory conditions and wound healing)
- MOTS-c (Reviewed for obesity and osteoporosis)
- Semax (Reviewed for cerebral ischemia/stroke, migraines, and trigeminal neuralgia)
- Epitalon (Reviewed primarily for insomnia)
- Emideltide / DSIP (Delta Sleep-Inducing Peptide; reviewed for chronic insomnia, narcolepsy, and opioid withdrawal)

Doing so will not stop patient demand or clinical use; it will drive patients to unregulated sources that present substantially greater safety risks. That outcome conflicts directly with the public-health priorities repeatedly emphasized by HHS leadership.

Key points for your consideration:

Patient safety: When regulated compounding pharmacies are prevented from legally supplying needed preparations, patients commonly turn to online “research chemical” vendors and black-market suppliers. These products frequently lack identity verification, potency testing, sterility assurance, and lot-traceability. The result is increased risk of contamination, incorrect dosing, inadvertent exposure to toxins or undeclared substances, and treatment failures.

Regulatory safeguards vs. no safeguards: 503A compounding operates under state-board oversight and federal guidance, enforces prescription-based dispensing tied to a prescriber–patient relationship, and can be held accountable through licensure, inspections, USP standards (sterile compounding), and adverse-event reporting. Removing legal access eliminates those layers of protection rather than adding meaningful public-health benefit.

Aligns with HHS concerns: HHS has repeatedly prioritized reducing avoidable harms from unregulated drug supply chains and promoting safe, evidence-based care. Restricting compounding in a way that funnels patients to illicit markets undermines those policy objectives and increases the very harms the agency seeks to prevent.

Practical safeguards that preserve safety: If there are specific, evidence-based concerns about certain peptides, address those directly through targeted measures—required testing, clear labeling, mandatory lot documentation, enhanced adverse-event surveillance, limits tied to an established prescriber–patient relationship, and robust inspection/enforcement—rather than blanket bans that create unsafe demand.

Recommendation: Reject broad prohibitions that close off regulated compounding access. Instead, adopt narrowly tailored regulatory controls that maintain patient access through accountable, inspected pharmacies while strengthening testing, documentation, and reporting requirements to mitigate risks.

Thank you for prioritizing patient safety and predictable regulatory oversight in your deliberations.

title: Comment from Anonymous
comment:
Re: Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895
Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee Meeting — July 23–24, 2026
I am submitting this comment as a health and fitness professional who works with adults pursuing improved metabolic health, physical function, and long-term wellness. I respectfully encourage the Committee and FDA to consider maintaining a carefully controlled, patient-specific pathway for appropriately qualified prescribers and state-licensed compounding pharmacies to evaluate and use certain bulk drug substances under Section 503A when clinically appropriate. My comment is not intended to represent that any specific substance is FDA-approved, proven effective for any condition, or appropriate for unsupervised use. I recognize that compounded drug products are not FDA-approved and that the available human safety, pharmacology, quality, and efficacy data for several of the substances under review may be limited. However, restricting access without a clear regulated pathway may unintentionally shift demand toward poorly controlled channels, including products marketed for research use, products of uncertain identity or purity, or self-directed use without appropriate medical screening, informed consent, product-quality controls, or adverse-event monitoring.
Where FDA determines that a substance can meet the statutory and scientific standards for inclusion on the 503A Bulks List, I encourage the Agency to support a framework that emphasizes:
* patient-specific prescribing by appropriately licensed clinicians;
* use only by qualifying state-licensed compounding pharmacies;
* robust active pharmaceutical ingredient identity, purity, sterility, endotoxin, and lot-release testing where applicable;
* clear informed-consent procedures addressing uncertainty, potential risks, and the non-FDA-approved status of compounded products;
* appropriate patient screening, clinical follow-up, and adverse-event reporting;
* restrictions against misleading consumer marketing or unsupported disease-treatment claims; and
* continued review as higher-quality human safety and clinical data become available.
A transparent, medically supervised, quality-controlled pathway is preferable to driving patients toward unregulated or inadequately supervised sources. FDA should continue applying rigorous scientific standards, while also considering the public-health consequences of eliminating lawful clinical oversight where patients may still seek access through less accountable channels.
Thank you for considering this perspective.

title: Comment from Mills John
comment:
I respectfully request that these compounds remain accessible. Many have successfully resolved longstanding health issues for me that credentialed medical professionals were unwilling or unable to address. The rapid expansion of information, user experiences, and community feedback—particularly regarding grey-market sources—has become substantial. Peptide testing groups have also proliferated, enabling collective efforts to verify purity, identify contaminants, confirm dosing accuracy, and enhance overall safety. For many individuals, pooling resources for independent testing represents the most practical path forward, as the traditional prescription or compounding pharmacy route remains prohibitively expensive and time-intensive.

Sure, these compounds like anything else have both good and bad aspects. Let's not forget the illusion of safety we've existed in for decades.

Scientific integrity failures: Publication bias, funding conflicts & hidden risks caused massive harm. Beyond the sugar-fat scam & Alzheimer’s image fraud:

Thalidomide (birth defects)
Vioxx (heart attacks/strokes)
Fen-Phen (heart valve damage)
Paxil (suicide risk in kids)
OxyContin (addiction epidemic)
DES (cancers in offspring)
Seroquel/Zyprexa (hidden diabetes)
Rimonabant (psychiatric harm)
CAST antiarrhythmics (~100k deaths)
Boldt’s fabricated trials

Estimates of U.S. deaths from medical errors in hospitals range from ~250,000 (often cited as the third leading cause of death after heart disease and cancer) to as high as ~440,000 per year when including broader preventable harms. These figures come from analyses like those in BMJ and Journal of Patient Safety, though exact numbers are debated due to underreporting on death certificates.

This is just a short list.

Given that conflicting expert opinions can be found on nearly any medical topic, individuals are often left to navigate complex risk-benefit decisions on their own, effectively assuming a greater role in managing their own care. This reality does not justify eliminating access to potentially beneficial options; by the same logic, we would ban private vehicles to prevent traffic accidents.

title: Comment from Pagel Jorden
comment:
My name is Jorden Pagel. I'm a certified wellness consultant and health coach with over a decade of experience, and I've spent the last two years using several of the compounds under review — personally, on my own body, tracked. I'm writing because the people making these decisions should hear from someone who actually used the stuff, not just the abstract of a mouse study.

Start with the GLP-1s, because that's the one that isn't close.

Tirzepatide and retatrutide changed my life. I don't say that the way a brochure says it. I mean I spent the better part of a decade fighting my own body, losing, and getting up to lose again the next morning. These drugs gave me back something I'd basically written off. The weight came off. But that's not even the part that matters most — the part that matters is I feel like myself again. If you've never lost that, I can't explain it to you. If you have, I don't need to.

Reta wasn't free of cost, and I'll be straight about that, because a comment that pretends otherwise is worthless to you. Both times I ran it my resting heart rate climbed and my anxiety came up with it. I felt it. I tracked it. I came off to watch those numbers walk back down. That's exactly the point, though — I *knew* to watch, because I was working with real information and paying attention. The answer to a side effect like that isn't to shove the whole category into a back alley. It's supervision. It's access with a coach and a plan, which is the opposite of what shutting down 503A compounding gets you.

MOTS-c was the surprise. I didn't expect much and it turned out to be one of the better things I ran all year — energy up, recovery noticeably better, the kind of difference you feel in a training session and not just on a spreadsheet. Is the human research early? Yes. I've read it. I know what it is and isn't. But I'm one of the humans, and it did something real for me.

Then BPC-157, which is the one I'd fight hardest for.

I had an elbow that wouldn't quit. Ran BPC locally, 250mcg a day, five weeks, right into the joint that was giving me trouble. The nagging backed off. And there's an ankle — bothered me for over a year, the kind of thing you stop mentioning because you've made peace with it — that quietly stopped bothering me somewhere in the middle of all this. No rehab. No focused work on it. Can I hand you a clean line proving the peptide did it? No. I won't pretend I can. But I lived in that body for the year and the timing wasn't nothing.

Here's what I actually want to say to whoever reads this.

I am not a reckless person. I tracked my sleep against an Oura ring night after night. I logged doses. I noted what worked, and — this is the part the marketing crowd leaves out — I noted what *didn't*. Some of these compounds did nothing for me. I said so, out loud, to the people I coach. That's what responsible access looks like. Not a free-for-all. Not snake oil. People paying attention, keeping records, using real products from real compounding pharmacies instead of whatever shows up in an unmarked vial from overseas when the legal supply gets cut off.

Because that's the actual choice in front of you. It isn't "these compounds exist" versus "they don't." They exist. People are using them right now, today, in numbers that aren't going down. The only thing 503A restriction decides is whether they get them from a pharmacy with quality control and a certificate of analysis, or from the gray market where nobody's testing anything and the label is a guess. I've watched that gray market up close. Pulling the regulated option doesn't protect anyone. It just hands the whole thing to the people doing it worst.

Keep the access. Keep it supervised, keep it tested, keep it legal. That's the version that actually keeps people safe.

Thank you for reading a real account from a real person who used these and is better for it.

Jorden Pagel

The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee has a historic opportunity on July 23, 2026, to restore safe, legal access to peptide therapies that millions of Americans already seek. I also seek them. The only question is whether they will find them through regulated channels or unregulated ones. When the FDA placed these substances on its Category 2 restricted list in 2023, it did not eliminate demand; it redirected patients toward an entirely uncontrolled black market of so-called "research peptides" that carry no sterility requirements, no batch records, no endotoxin testing, and no recall system — products that are, by the seller's own admission, "not for human consumption." This prohibition did not protect consumers but instead drove them toward "very, very substandard" ingredients produced without any pharmaceutical oversight. Adding these substances to the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List would bring them back under the authority of licensed compounding pharmacies operating in ISO-classified cleanrooms, using FDA-registered ingredient suppliers with verified Certificates of Analysis, and following USP <797> sterile preparation standards for every injectable product. That is not loosening oversight — it is restoring it.

Compounded peptide medications, prepared by licensed 503A pharmacies under a valid patient-specific prescription, represent exactly the kind of individualized, physician-supervised care that compounding law was designed to protect. Peptides currently under PCAC review — including BPC-157 for ulcerative colitis and inflammatory conditions, TB-500 for wound healing, MOTS-c for obesity and osteoporosis, and Emideltide for opioid withdrawal and insomnia — address serious, underserved medical needs where commercially available alternatives are limited or unavailable. Licensed compounding pharmacies are already subject to rigorous state board oversight, and each sterile injectable peptide must pass sterility testing, potency verification, and endotoxin screening before reaching a patient. A favorable PCAC recommendation on July 23 would not grant blanket approval; it would simply initiate a formal notice-and-comment rulemaking process — the careful, deliberate pathway that the law requires before any substance may be added to the compounding list. To deny this pathway is to deny patients safe access while doing nothing to stop the unregulated alternatives that will fill the void.

Please vote to restore access to these peptides!

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee Meeting — July 23–24, 2026
I am submitting this comment as a health and fitness professional who works with adults pursuing improved metabolic health, physical function, and long-term wellness. I respectfully encourage the Committee and FDA to consider maintaining a carefully controlled, patient-specific pathway for appropriately qualified prescribers and state-licensed compounding pharmacies to evaluate and use certain bulk drug substances under Section 503A when clinically appropriate. My comment is not intended to represent that any specific substance is FDA-approved, proven effective for any condition, or appropriate for unsupervised use. I recognize that compounded drug products are not FDA-approved and that the available human safety, pharmacology, quality, and efficacy data for several of the substances under review may be limited. Where FDA determines that a substance can meet the statutory and scientific standards for inclusion on the 503A Bulks List, I encourage the Agency to support a framework that emphasizes:
* patient-specific prescribing by appropriately licensed clinicians;
* use only by qualifying state-licensed compounding pharmacies;
* robust active pharmaceutical ingredient identity, purity, sterility, endotoxin, and lot-release testing where applicable;
* clear informed-consent procedures addressing uncertainty, potential risks, and the non-FDA-approved status of compounded products;
* appropriate patient screening, clinical follow-up, and adverse-event reporting;
* restrictions against misleading consumer marketing or unsupported disease-treatment claims; and
* continued review as higher-quality human safety and clinical data become available.
A transparent, medically supervised, quality-controlled pathway is preferable to driving patients toward unregulated or inadequately supervised sources. To the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee and FDA:

I am writing in strong support of removing appropriate peptide bulk drug substances from Category 2 and allowing them to be considered for inclusion on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List.

Peptides such as BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax, Epitalon, and DSIP-related compounds are not fringe products. They are biologically active signaling molecules that have been used by many licensed medical providers as part of individualized, patient-specific care. In clinical practice, these compounds are often used to support areas where conventional medicine has limited options, including tissue repair, inflammation modulation, metabolic support, sleep regulation, neurologic support, and recovery.

The current restriction has not eliminated demand. It has pushed patients and providers toward a less safe marketplace. When legitimate 503A compounding pharmacies are unable to prepare these products pursuant to a valid prescription, patients often turn to unregulated online sellers, foreign sources, or “research use only” products with unknown purity, potency, sterility, and sourcing. That is not safer for the public. It is more dangerous.

A regulated compounding pathway is the more responsible option. Licensed 503A pharmacies operate under state board oversight, require patient-specific prescriptions, source ingredients through appropriate channels, and compound according to professional standards. This is meaningfully different from the gray market, where patients may self-dose products of unknown quality without medical supervision.

It is also important to put risk into perspective. Many medications currently available in the U.S. market carry significant known risks, including black box warnings, organ toxicity, dependency risk, metabolic harm, immune suppression, and serious adverse event profiles. By comparison, many of these peptides have demonstrated practical clinical utility with what appears to be a favorable safety profile when they are properly sourced, properly compounded, properly prescribed, and properly monitored.

The appropriate response to uncertainty should not be prohibition. It should be standards. FDA should create a clear, lawful, regulated framework that allows qualified prescribers and compounding pharmacies to serve patients responsibly. This framework could include quality requirements, documentation standards, appropriate labeling, sterility expectations, adverse event reporting, and clinical-use guardrails.

Removing these substances from Category 2 and allowing consideration for the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List would protect patients, support provider discretion, and reduce reliance on unregulated products. Patients deserve access to individualized therapies through lawful medical channels, not through the black market.

I respectfully urge the Committee and FDA to support appropriate peptide access through regulated 503A compounding rather than continued restriction. These products can do significant good when used responsibly, and in many cases may be safer than numerous medications already permitted in the marketplace.

title: Comment from Anonymous
comment:
SUBMISSION TO: FDA Public Docket No. FDA-2025-N-6895
RE: July 23–24, 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee Meeting – Bulk Drug Substances for the 503A Bulks List
DATE: 7/3/2026
To the Members of the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee:
As a registered nurse with over two decades of clinical experience, I strongly support the inclusion of BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon on the 503A Bulks List to ensure patients can access these therapies safely through regulated healthcare channels.
Regardless of regulatory status, many patients seek these peptides. When they are not available through licensed providers and regulated pharmacies, individuals may turn to online vendors, overseas suppliers, or products marketed as research chemicals, which often lack reliable quality controls, sterility standards, and ingredient verification.
Obtaining these therapies through a legitimate healthcare process allows for appropriate evaluation, informed consent, and ongoing monitoring by licensed professionals. Access through a state-licensed 503A compounding pharmacy offers accountability and quality assurance not found in many alternative sources.
While questions remain regarding clinical evidence and long-term safety, restricting access may drive patients toward unregulated markets. Allowing access within a regulated framework enables healthcare providers to monitor outcomes and pharmacies to adhere to established standards.
Several of these peptides continue to generate scientific interest for their potential roles in tissue repair, gastrointestinal health, metabolic function, mitochondrial health, recovery, sleep regulation, and cognitive performance. Although additional research is warranted, there is interest in exploring these therapies under medical supervision.
If these substances are considered for inclusion on the 503A Bulks List, I encourage emphasis on safeguards such as:
• Sourcing ingredients from qualified suppliers with appropriate quality documentation.
• Adherence to applicable sterile compounding standards.
• Patient-specific prescriptions issued by licensed prescribers.
• Ongoing adverse-event reporting and quality monitoring.
• Transparency regarding product testing and quality assurance measures.
Patients will continue to seek these therapies regardless of regulatory barriers, and denying regulated access only increases the likelihood that they will turn to unsafe, unverified sources. The central issue is not whether access exists, but whether it occurs within a framework that prioritizes patient safety, clinical oversight, and product integrity. Inclusion of these substances on the 503A Bulks List would provide a controlled, accountable pathway that protects patients while allowing responsible medical use. I strongly urge the Committee to support their inclusion and to reinforce a regulatory approach that safeguards public health rather than inadvertently driving patients toward greater risk.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments.
Respectfully submitted,
BSN, RN
California Registered Nurse

comment:

State: Texas
Profession: Physician (MD)

I am a licensed physician (MD) practicing in Texas with a clinical focus in hormone replacement therapy, metabolic health, weight management, wellness medicine, longevity, and supervised use of peptide-based and micronutrient therapies.

This demand is most commonly driven by individuals with chronic conditions or persistent symptoms who report incomplete response to standard therapies.

Over the past six months, I have increasingly encountered patients who report obtaining these compounds through non-medical vendors and unregulated online sources. This raises public health concerns related to product quality, sterility, dosing accuracy, and lack of clinical oversight.

From a safety and regulatory perspective, the current environment may be contributing to increased utilization of unregulated supply chains for peptide products. This creates challenges for clinicians in ensuring appropriate monitoring, adverse event tracking, and consistent product quality.

Inclusion of appropriate peptide substances on the 503A Bulks List may support patient safety by enabling physician-supervised compounding, standardized preparation, and structured clinical monitoring, while reducing reliance on unregulated and potentially variable sources.

I encourage the Committee to consider the real-world clinical environment in which these compounds are already being sought and used, alongside the current limitations of the published evidence base, when evaluating regulatory pathways for compounded peptide substances.

title: Comment from Ripley Adam
comment:
I am submitting this comment in connection with the upcoming Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting on July 23–24, 2026, at which the Committee will evaluate whether BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon should be added to the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List. I am a board-certified clinical pharmacist, PharmD, and pharmacy executive with a professional background in compliance and accreditation leadership, including direct experience with USP <795>, <797>, and <800> compounding standards, and with peptide and metabolic medicine practice. In this capacity, I have observed firsthand both the value that appropriately compounded peptide therapies provide to patients under physician supervision, and the compliance infrastructure that accredited 503A pharmacies maintain to ensure their safe preparation and dispensing. I have also witnessed the widespread problems caused by pushing peptide access away from the provider-pharmacist-patient relationship and toward unregulated research and grey markets with zero oversight and no provider guidance to patients.

Compounded peptides prepared under Section 503A are subject to a layered oversight framework that unregulated sources are not: state board of pharmacy licensure, adherence to USP <795> and <797> standards for non-sterile and sterile compounding, ingredient sourcing and identity testing, batch documentation, and a valid patient-specific prescription issued by a supervising physician. This structure creates accountability at every step — from raw material to finished preparation to the prescribing relationship — that is simply absent in the direct-to-consumer "research chemical" market that has grown around these same peptides.

We have to start by fixing the supply chain for peptides. Making them eligible under 503A immediately taps into multi-layered oversight, from compliant raw-material API sourcing all the way through validated testing of the end product before a patient receives their prescription. The peptides currently before this Committee have none of these safeguards for patients — zero. If this process is truly about patient safety, we have to start with the supply chain. We already have the proper infrastructure in place: 503A compounding pharmacies have supported providers and patients for decades.

When compounding access is restricted without a corresponding approved commercial alternative, demand does not disappear — it migrates to the unregulated market, where there is no verification of identity, purity, sterility, or dosing accuracy, and no prescriber oversight. Restricting the legitimate 503A pathway does not eliminate patient exposure to these substances; it removes the safeguards around that exposure and puts patients at risk every day. I believe this dynamic is directly relevant to the Committee's risk-benefit analysis for each peptide under review. Compounded peptides prescribed and monitored by a physician provide an individualized treatment option within a supervised clinical relationship. Removing that option does not remove the underlying clinical need — it removes the physician's ability to meet that need through an accountable channel, and it disproportionately burdens patients who cannot access off-label alternatives or who have already found a compounded formulation effective and well-tolerated under monitoring.
Do we need more outcomes data for these peptides? Yes — the industry acknowledges that need. We can get there through properly sourced raw material, regulated and accountable 503A compounding, and provider-monitored therapy. Continuing to push patients toward unregulated access and use will never allow clinicians to generate the data we all agree is missing.

A well-regulated compounding pathway serves patients, physicians, and public health better than the alternative of pushing this demand into an unaccountable market. I urge the Committee to weigh the safety record of accredited 503A compounding, alongside the clinical and cost burdens that restriction places on patients, in reaching its recommendations.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment and for the Committee's careful consideration of this issue.

Respectfully submitted,
Adam Ripley, PharmD, RPh, FAAMFM, ABAAHP
Seattle, Washington

title: Comment from Gerald Mestas
comment:
**Comment**

I am submitting this comment as an individual in support of maintaining patient access to pharmacy-compounded peptides when prescribed by a licensed healthcare provider and prepared by qualified compounding pharmacies that meet applicable quality standards.

Many patients rely on compounded medications because commercially available products may not meet their individual medical needs. Personalized dosing, formulation, and treatment plans are important aspects of individualized medicine. Restricting access to compounded peptide therapies without carefully evaluating the available scientific literature, physician experience, and patient outcomes may unnecessarily limit treatment options for patients who have few alternatives.

Peptides have been the subject of extensive scientific research over several decades. While not every peptide has the same level of clinical evidence, each substance should be evaluated individually based on its pharmacology, safety profile, available human data, published research, and documented clinical experience. A broad approach that treats all peptides similarly may overlook meaningful differences between compounds.

I encourage the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee to consider:

* Published peer-reviewed scientific literature.
* Clinical experience from licensed physicians who prescribe these therapies responsibly.
* Patient-reported outcomes and quality-of-life improvements.
* The importance of individualized medicine through licensed compounding pharmacies.
* The potential impact on patients if medically supervised access is significantly reduced.

Compounded medications have long served an important role when commercially manufactured products cannot adequately meet individual patient needs. Appropriate regulation should continue to prioritize product quality, sterility, accurate labeling, and patient safety while preserving access to therapies that physicians determine are medically appropriate.

I respectfully request that FDA evaluate each nominated bulk drug substance on its own scientific merits and allow appropriately supported peptide substances to remain available for compounding when they meet the statutory criteria under Section 503A. A balanced, evidence-based approach can protect public health while preserving physician judgment and patient access to individualized care.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment from Newmen Law P.C.
comment:
Newmen Law, P.C. is a California law firm that represents businesses and individuals across the pharmacy compounding and peptide sector. We submit this comment in support of adding all seven nominated peptides (BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide/DSIP, Semax, and Epitalon) to the Section 503A Bulks List, subject to reasonable conditions. Our position rests on consumer protection.

The question before the Committee is not whether Americans will use these peptides. They already do, in very large numbers. The real question is whether that use occurs through licensed pharmacies and physicians, with tested ingredients and oversight, or through an unregulated research-use-only (RUO) and direct-to-consumer grey market. Prohibition has not reduced demand. It has pushed consumers toward the least safe channel.

The scale is not theoretical. Aggregate, anonymized data reported to the firm by its clients reflects roughly 122,400 orders and 373,363 units over about eighteen months (late 2024 through mid 2026), an estimated 3.7 to 7.5 million individual doses. Across that entire volume, the data reflects twelve customer complaints in total. Ten described mild reactions such as injection-site irritation, rash, or allergic reaction, and two were non-health complaints. No serious adverse event was reported.

We do not offer that number as proof of safety, and we urge the Committee not to read it that way. The RUO channel has no clinical relationship with the purchaser and no pharmacovigilance system, so reported complaints necessarily understate true incidence. That is the point. The unregulated channel cannot generate the safety data FDA wants, cannot assure identity, purity, potency, or sterility, and cannot supervise the patient. A regulated 503A pathway can do all of these things. The grey-market harms that concern FDA, including contamination, mislabeling, inconsistent potency, and unsupervised self-injection, are artifacts of the channel, not properties of the molecules.

The governing standard supports placement. Section 503A directs FDA to weigh four considerations: physical and chemical characterization, safety, effectiveness or the lack of it, and historical use in compounding. This is a balancing test, not the new-drug-approval bar. The absence of large modern trials is not a finding that a substance is ineffective, and FDA may list a substance on the balance of these factors. FDA's stated concerns for these peptides, including
potential immunogenicity, peptide-related impurities, and limited safety information, are statements about product quality and data gaps. A regulated pathway with defined controls answers each of them directly.

We therefore urge the Committee to recommend placement, subject to conditions that define a responsible pathway and separate it from the grey market:
1. Compounding only on a valid, patient-specific prescription;
2. Licensed-prescriber oversight within a bona fide prescriber-patient relationship;
3. Active ingredient from FDA-registered suppliers, with identity, purity, and potency testing and a certificate of analysis;
4. Sterility and endotoxin testing for injectable preparations;
5. Systematic adverse-event reporting, the safety surveillance the grey market lacks; and
6. No direct-to-consumer sale and no use of RUO product in humans outside the pharmacy channel.

Forcing patients into the black and grey market is not the safest path. It is the most dangerous one. Placement of these substances on the 503A list, under the conditions above, would replace an unregulated channel with licensed, accountable, patient-specific care. That result protects consumers.
A supporting legal memorandum and the underlying distribution and complaint data are submitted as attachments to this comment.

Respectfully submitted,
Kaveh Newmen, Esq.
Newmen Law, P.C., Santa Ana, California

I am the owner and primary provider at a medical aesthetics and wellness clinic in Fayetteville, North Carolina, where I treat a patient population that includes a significant number of active-duty military and veterans from the nearby Fort Liberty community. I write in strong support of restoring a legal, regulated compounding pathway for BPC-157, TB-500, and the other peptides under review at this month's hearing.
I served 32 years in the United States Army, 10 of those as a Special Forces 18D Medical Sergeant, and the remaining 22 as a Physician Assistant, including three combat tours: Desert Shield/Storm, OIF1, and OEF10. I understand what these compounds are being asked to do in the body, both from the standpoint of a medic who has treated injury under fire and a clinician who has spent a career managing recovery, pain, and long-term physical wear. I understand what it means to ask a body to keep performing after decades of accumulated demand.
At 57, I am doing things physically — endurance events, mountaineering, sustained high-output training — that I could not do at 27. Peptide therapy, administered under my own clinical judgment and monitoring, has been a material part of that change. This is not a marginal or cosmetic benefit. It is the difference between a body that is breaking down and one that is still capable of demanding work.
I see the same pattern daily in my patients: measurable improvements in tissue repair, recovery time, and functional capacity, without the adverse event profile the FDA is right to scrutinize in genuinely dangerous compounds. I do not say that lightly. I have spent real time evaluating the safety literature on these peptides, including the tumor-risk questions raised about BPC-157 and TB-500, and I do not believe the evidence supports the level of restriction these compounds have faced.
The FDA devotes significant enforcement attention to substances with far weaker safety records and far less demonstrated benefit than the peptides on this docket. When placed in the hands of licensed, trained healthcare providers who understand dosing, sourcing, and patient selection, these are not the compounds that belong on a list of genuine public health threats. Removing the legal 503A compounding pathway does not eliminate demand or use — it eliminates oversight, quality control, and the physician relationship that makes these therapies safe in the first place.
I urge the Committee to recommend BPC-157, TB-500, and the associated peptides under review for inclusion on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List.
Respectfully,
Dr. Scott T. Festa, DMSc, APA-C

title: Comment from Michael Tessitore
comment:
I write in support of including the following peptides on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances list, so licensed compounding pharmacies may prepare them pursuant to a valid patient-specific prescription. Each is discussed on its own merits below.
BPC-157. A synthetic pentadecapeptide derived from a gastric-juice sequence, proposed to act via angiogenesis (including VEGFR2 signaling) and nitric oxide modulation. Substantial preclinical work supports accelerated healing of tendon, ligament, muscle, and gastrointestinal tissue, with a favorable observed safety margin.
KPV. A C-terminal tripeptide fragment of α-MSH with anti-inflammatory effects via downregulation of NF-κB-mediated signaling and associated cytokines — relevant to conditions such as ulcerative colitis and inflammation-impaired wound healing.
TB-500. A synthetic peptide corresponding to the active region of Thymosin β4, promoting cell migration, actin remodeling, and angiogenesis, underlying its studied role in wound healing and soft-tissue repair.
MOTS-c. A mitochondrial-derived peptide proposed to activate AMPK signaling and improve insulin sensitivity and metabolic and exercise capacity.
DSIP (Emideltide). A nonapeptide implicated in regulating sleep architecture and neuroendocrine function, of clinical interest for insomnia and sleep quality.
Semax. A synthetic ACTH(4–10) analog with neuroprotective and nootropic activity attributed to modulation of BDNF and NGF expression.
Epitalon. A synthetic tetrapeptide analog of the pineal peptide epithalamin, studied preclinically for circadian and melatonin regulation and telomerase- and aging-related endpoints.
Shared safety rationale. These are short-chain peptides with rapid enzymatic degradation and predictable pharmacokinetics. Their mechanisms do not implicate the toxicity pathways that raise categorical safety concerns, and available preclinical and real-world data are consistent with favorable safety profiles at therapeutic doses under physician supervision.
Clinical experience. In my own experience over several months, a compounded blend containing BPC-157, TB-500, and KPV (marketed as "KLOW," which also contains GHK-Cu) produced meaningful, consistent quality-of-life improvements. Everyday minor aches in my neck and back diminished noticeably, as did wrist and forearm pain from long hours at a computer — consistent with the soft-tissue repair mechanisms of BPC-157 and TB-500. I also saw a marked reduction in gastrointestinal symptoms I had previously associated with IBS, consistent with the gastroprotective and anti-inflammatory mechanisms of BPC-157 and KPV. As a blend I cannot isolate a single component, but the improvements align with its constituents' established mechanisms and were sustained across repeated cycles without adverse events.
I have also recently begun using DSIP for sleep. It is early — only a few weeks — so I offer this as a preliminary observation, not an established outcome: my wearable tracker shows deep sleep becoming more consolidated toward the beginning of the night rather than spread evenly across it, with a corresponding difference in how rested I feel. This reflects the individualized response that supports continued patient access under physician supervision.
Regulatory context. These substances were moved to Category 2 in 2023–2024 largely on administrative and evidentiary gaps rather than affirmative safety findings, and the intervening years have produced additional data. Restoring 503A eligibility does not equate to FDA approval; it restores a physician's ability to prescribe, and a pharmacy's ability to compound, on an individualized basis with that framework's accountability. Continued prohibition instead pushes patients toward unregulated, research-only, and grey-market sources with no pharmacy oversight — the worse safety outcome.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Committee to recommend inclusion of these peptides on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances list.
Respectfully,
Respectfully,
Michael Tessitore III
Clifton Park, NY

title: Comment from Jones Kevin
comment:
To the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee:

I am a licensed physician who regularly treats patients seeking evidence-informed options to support recovery, metabolic health, healthy aging, and overall wellness. I am writing in support of maintaining a regulated compounding pathway for peptides such as BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon while additional research continues to evolve.

In clinical practice, many patients experience significant unmet needs that are not adequately addressed by currently approved therapies alone. Patients recovering from injuries, managing age-related decline in function, seeking support for metabolic health, or looking for options to improve quality of life frequently ask about peptide therapies. A regulated compounding pathway allows licensed healthcare providers to evaluate patients individually, discuss known risks and limitations, obtain informed consent, and prescribe these therapies through state-licensed compounding pharmacies operating under established quality and safety standards.

Eliminating access to compounded peptide therapies would not eliminate patient demand. Instead, it risks driving patients toward unregulated online sources, research-grade products, or international suppliers where product quality, sterility, dosing accuracy, and clinical oversight may be uncertain. Maintaining an appropriate regulatory pathway helps ensure patients receive medical evaluation, ongoing monitoring, and products prepared by licensed pharmacies that are subject to regulatory oversight.

While additional clinical research is warranted for many peptide therapies, the existence of ongoing scientific uncertainty should not automatically preclude access through physician-directed compounding. Historically, compounding has played an important role in addressing individual patient needs when commercially available treatment options are limited or unavailable. Preserving a regulated pathway allows clinicians to exercise professional judgment while supporting patient safety, informed decision-making, and continued collection of real-world clinical experience.

I respectfully encourage the Committee to consider the practical impact these decisions will have on patient access, provider oversight, and public safety. A carefully regulated compounding framework offers a safer alternative to unregulated markets while preserving important treatment options for appropriately selected patients.

Thank you for your consideration. Kevin Jones, MD

title: Comment from BOUFFARD MICHAEL
