I am writing to express my strong support for preserving patient and physician access to compounded peptides prepared by licensed, accredited compounding pharmacies operating under established state and federal regulatory oversight.

For many patients, compounded peptides are not a luxury—they are an important component of individualized medical care. Physicians rely on these medications when commercially available products do not adequately meet a patient’s unique clinical needs, and pharmacists play a critical role in preparing these medications according to rigorous quality and safety standards. This collaborative patient-physician-pharmacist relationship is a cornerstone of personalized medicine.

Restricting access to compounded peptides would have significant unintended consequences. Rather than eliminating demand, it would drive many patients toward unregulated domestic and international gray markets where products are frequently manufactured without meaningful quality controls, sterility testing, potency verification, or accountability. Such a shift would expose patients to substantially greater health risks while undermining the very public safety objectives these restrictions seek to achieve.

Reduced access would disproportionately affect individuals managing chronic medical conditions, those on fixed incomes, veterans, retirees, and others who already face significant financial barriers to care. Maintaining a regulated compounding pathway helps ensure that safe, affordable treatment options remain available through licensed healthcare professionals instead of forcing patients to seek less reliable alternatives.

Licensed compounding pharmacies are already subject to extensive oversight through state boards of pharmacy, applicable federal regulations, accreditation standards, and quality assurance requirements. Rather than restricting responsible providers who operate within these safeguards, regulatory efforts should focus on strengthening compliance, enforcing existing standards, and eliminating bad actors who fail to meet appropriate quality and safety expectations.

I respectfully urge the committee to preserve and strengthen a safe, transparent, and well-regulated pathway for compounded peptides. Doing so protects patient safety, supports physician judgment, preserves the patient-provider relationship, promotes access to individualized care, and keeps patients within accountable healthcare channels instead of driving them into the unregulated marketplace.

title: Comment from Amil Patel
comment:
My name is Amil Patel, and I am a pharmacist. I am writing in support of adding the nominated peptides to the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, with appropriate safeguards around prescriptions, physician oversight, licensed pharmacy compounding, pharmacist counseling, and adverse-event and outcomes reporting.

I came to pharmacy through compounding. My first job in High School was at Skywalk Pharmacy, an independent pediatric compounding pharmacy connected to Children’s Hospital of Wisconsin. I remember parents coming in because the medicine their child needed existed, but not in a form that worked for their child. Sometimes the issue was strength, taste, excipients, a feeding tube, or a dosage form a child could not take - these details were the difference between a treatment being usable or not.

That experience fundamentally shaped how I think about pharmacy. Medication access is not only about whether a molecule exists or whether it appears in a guideline. It is also about whether a patient can actually use it safely and consistently in the context of their life.

Since then, I have helped launch and scale one of the largest digital pharmacies in the US, and I have also helped launch a pharmacy benefits manager. Those experiences gave me a broader view of the same problem. Our system can do remarkable things at scale, but I have also seen how often patients are forced through rules and incentives that are only loosely connected to their needs: coverage restrictions, prior authorizations, formulary exclusions, rebate structures, and delays.

For someone in pain, recovering from injury, or dealing with chronic symptoms that have not responded well to available options, time is not abstract. Being told to wait for evidence that no one has a commercial incentive to generate is not a neutral position, in fact to patients it feels like a punishment for being sick!

I understand the concern about evidence, I share it as a pharmacist. I don't want patients using poor-quality products, guessing at doses, interpreting labs they aren't trained to interpret, or using substances without medical oversight. But excluding these substances from regulated compounding has not eliminated demand at all. It has pushed that demand into channels that are harder to supervise.

Patients are already seeking these compounds through research-use-only websites, overseas suppliers, online forums, private communities, and gray-market vendors. They are trying to determine for themselves whether a peptide is authentic, whether a certificate of analysis is meaningful, whether the dose is appropriate, and whether a product is safe to use. Do we think the Patient ought to carry this burden? Is this the system we want to leave behind for our children?

A 503A pathway would not answer every scientific question about these peptides. It would not mean every proposed use is proven. What it would do is move use into a setting where safeguards can operate: a patient-specific prescription, a prescriber responsible for the clinical decision, a licensed pharmacy responsible for sourcing and compounding, a pharmacist available for counseling, records that can be reviewed, and adverse events that can be reported. It would also create the possibility of collecting structured outcomes over time.

There is precedent for medicine learning this way. Pediatrics is one example that feels especially relevant to me because of where I started. For many years, children were treated with medications that lacked the pediatric-specific evidence and labeling we would expect today. Clinicians still had to care for the children in front of them. Over time, the system created better mechanisms: pediatric study requirements, labeling updates, improved formulations, and more systematic learning from use. That history does not argue for lowering standards, it shows that when unmet need exists - supervised use and evidence generation can be brought closer together.

If the nominated peptides are added to the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List, access can be paired with conditions that make sense for the risk: valid prescriptions, physician oversight, applicable USP standards, quality documentation, pharmacist counseling, adverse-event reporting, and structured outcomes tracking. This would allow us to at least *attempt* to reduce the evidence gap.

I became a pharmacist because I saw how much suffering can be relieved when medication use is made practical, individualized, and safe. Patients need standards, but they also need a system willing to engage with their needs before they are forced to solve the problem alone.

I urge the Committee to add the nominated peptides to the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List with appropriate safeguards, and to use that pathway to support the documentation, counseling, adverse-event reporting, and outcomes tracking that the current gray market cannot provide.

Respectfully,
Amil Patel, PharmD

title: Comment from Christopher Ortiz
comment:
To the Members of the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee and the Food and Drug Administration:
I am writing to formally submit my public comment in strong support of including the peptide-related bulk drug substances currently under evaluation—specifically BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon—on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List.
As a patient, I have witnessed firsthand the profound clinical utility and patient demand for these specific therapeutic options. Restricting access to these substances by omitting them from the 503A list would severely limit individualized patient care and have pushed patients toward unregulated, unsafe gray-market channels.
I urge the Committee to consider the following critical points during your July 23–24, 2026 deliberations:
Legitimate Clinical Need and Patient-Specific Care
Compounded medications are essential for patients who do not respond to mass-produced, commercially available FDA-approved drugs, or who require specific dosages or routes of administration. Peptides like BPC-157 and TB-500 are heavily relied upon for cellular repair and tissue recovery, while others like KPV and Semax offer targeted pathways for inflammation management and cognitive support. For many patients, these compounded formulations represent the only viable path to managing chronic or debilitating conditions.
The Danger of Restricting Monitored Medical Access
If licensed compounding pharmacies are prohibited from preparing these peptides under Section 503A, patient demand will not disappear. Instead, patients will continue to face a direct risk of sourcing these substances from unregulated online vendors, foreign suppliers, or products labeled "for research use only" that entirely lack quality control, sterility verification, and clinical oversight. Allowing 503A compounding keeps these therapies within a highly regulated system under the supervision of qualified physicians and pharmacists.
Safety and Quality via Standardized Compounding
Rather than enforcing a blanket restriction due to limited large-scale human clinical trials, placing these peptides on the 503A Bulks List allows them to be prepared under strict USP <795> and <797> compounding standards. This ensures that patients receive pharmacy-grade, sterile, and accurately dosed medications rather than unverified alternatives.
I respectfully ask that the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee recommend the inclusion of BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide, Semax, and Epitalon on the Section 503A Bulk Drug Substances List. Preserving access to these compounded therapies under proper medical supervision is vital to protecting public health and ensuring patient choice.
Thank you for your time, scientific rigor, and consideration of this comment.
Sincerely,

Christopher Ortiz

title: Comment from Florie Brett
comment:
To the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee,

I am submitting this comment in support of including BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon on the 503A Bulks List, ahead of the July 23–24 committee meeting.

As a licensed physician with direct clinical experience prescribing several of these peptides, I have observed meaningful therapeutic benefit in my patients particularly in the areas of tissue repair, inflammation modulation, sleep regulation, and cognitive support. In my practice, BPC-157 and TB-500 have shown notable utility in patients with musculoskeletal injuries and delayed healing, often in cases where conventional options provided limited relief. Peptides such as Semax and Emideltide have offered a well-tolerated option for patients struggling with cognitive fatigue and sleep dysregulation.

Critically, the risk profiles I have observed in clinical use have been very low. These are not novel experimental compounds being introduced recklessly many have decades of research behind them and a track record of tolerability when dosed appropriately by trained providers. The greater risk, in my view, lies in the absence of a regulated compounding pathway. Without it, patients who benefit from these therapies face inconsistent quality, unreliable sourcing, and the loss of physician-supervised access entirely.

A regulated 503A compounding pathway does not expand risk it reduces it. It ensures standardized quality, proper labeling, and accountability within the supply chain, while preserving the individualized, patient-specific prescribing that defines good medical practice.

I respectfully urge the Committee to weigh the documented clinical utility of these peptides against the very real access gaps that exclusion would create for patients who have no comparable alternatives. The compounding pathway is not a workaround it is, for many of my patients, the only viable route to evidence-informed, physician-guided care.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit this comment for the record.

Respectfully,

Brett Florie DO
DEA FF0066957

title: Comment from Willis Ryan
comment:
Absolutely. Here’s the clean, copyable version with the individual component dosing included.

I am submitting this comment as a husband, father, and citizen who has personally witnessed the impact that compounded peptide access has had on my family’s life.

My wife is 39 years old and the mother of our three children, ages 3, 8, and 10. At an age when she should have been fully enjoying raising young children, she was instead living with severe chronic knee pain that affected nearly every aspect of her daily life.

After multiple MRIs and evaluations by multiple doctors, there was agreement that her knees were in such poor condition that she needed knee replacement surgery. At only 39 years old, we were facing the reality that double knee replacement surgery could be part of her near future.

There were days when she would cry because of the pain. Not occasionally, but almost daily.

Before using these compounds, there were evenings when my wife would sit in tears from knee pain while watching our children play because she physically could not join them. As her husband, that is one of the hardest things I have ever witnessed. Our children wanted their mother to run, play, and participate with them, but pain often dictated what she could and could not do.

Our children only get one childhood. There are no do-overs for missed moments.

My wife followed a structured 12-week regimen using a compounded peptide blend containing BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu, and KPV. Each vial contained 80 mg total peptide content: 50 mg GHK-Cu, 10 mg BPC-157, 10 mg TB-500, and 10 mg KPV. The vial was reconstituted with 3 mL of bacteriostatic water.

Her daily dose was 0.15 mL, which equals approximately 4 mg total peptide blend per day. Broken down by individual components, her approximate daily dose was:

GHK-Cu: 2.5 mg per day
BPC-157: 0.5 mg per day
TB-500: 0.5 mg per day
KPV: 0.5 mg per day

Over the full 12-week cycle, this equaled approximately:

GHK-Cu: 210 mg total
BPC-157: 42 mg total
TB-500: 42 mg total

title: Comment from Stahlschmidt William
comment:
I am writing in support of preserving a responsible, physician-supervised path for access to compounded therapeutic peptides.

My concern is fairly simple: when the FDA restricts access to compounds that patients and doctors believe may have real therapeutic value, demand does not disappear. If anything, demand appears to have surged after these compounds were excluded from the 503A Bulks List. Patients end up buying from “research chemical” websites, overseas vendors, or other sources with far less quality control and no meaningful medical supervision. Continuing the current policy does not make anyone safer. It just moves the risk somewhere harder to monitor.

I understand that many of these peptides do not have the kind of large, definitive clinical trials we would ideally want. Patients should not be told that these compounds are proven cures, and nobody should pretend the evidence is stronger than it is.

But limited data is not the same thing as clear evidence of danger. The widespread grey-market demand that has emerged also suggests that a simple access restriction has not solved the safety problem. If a compound has a strong signal of serious harm, then restriction may be justified. But in many cases, the concern appears to be incomplete evidence rather than demonstrated serious harm.

If the main issue is that the evidence is early, incomplete, or not yet developed to the standard required for full FDA approval, then the answer should not automatically be to remove access entirely. A better answer is to allow access through legitimate medical channels, with appropriate safeguards.

Many of these peptides are being explored for difficult problems like wound healing, inflammatory conditions, chronic injury, pain-related issues, sleep disorders, and other conditions where existing options are limited or entirely nonexistent. In some cases, these compounds may represent first-in-class therapeutic options where no approved treatment exists for a particular use. These are exactly the kinds of situations where patients and physicians need room to make individualized decisions.

Medicine is full of risk-benefit tradeoffs. The FDA should not assert that the only acceptable options are a fully approved commercial drug or nothing at all, depriving patients and doctors of the right to decide what is best for the individual in their specific medical context.

Compounding exists because real patients do not always fit neatly into standardized products. A physician who knows a patient’s history should be able to discuss the available evidence, the uncertainties, the potential risks, and the alternatives, and then decide whether a compounded option is reasonable. Patients should also have the right to participate in that decision. That is not reckless. That is normal patient-centered care.

The practical policy question should be: which approach creates the least overall harm while preserving reasonable patient and physician options for promising therapies with incomplete evidence?

A blanket restriction may look safer on paper. In reality, it pushes more patients toward unregulated products of unknown purity, unknown dose, and unknown sterility. By contrast, a legal compounding pathway allows for physician involvement, pharmacy standards, product testing, patient counseling, and adverse-event reporting. That is manifestly preferable to pretending the grey market will vanish through permanent restriction.

I would urge FDA to take the path that best supports responsible patient and physician access:

Allow appropriate peptides to remain available through legitimate compounding when prescribed by licensed clinicians for specific patients.

Require clear patient disclosure that these compounds are not FDA-approved and may have limited human data.

Focus heavily on ensuring ready access, with a prescription, to legitimate compounded products of known quality, sterility, purity, potency, and sourcing through U.S.-operated 503A facilities.

Encourage reporting of both beneficial and adverse events so real-world safety concerns can be tracked more effectively.

This approach would protect patients better than simply driving these compounds underground.

The FDA’s role should be to protect the public from unsafe products, poor manufacturing, and fraudulent claims. It should not unnecessarily prevent informed patients and licensed physicians from considering emerging therapeutic options, especially when the alternative is often unsupervised grey-market use.

A responsible framework is possible: regulated access, high quality standards, honest informed consent, physician supervision, and real-world safety monitoring.

I urge the Committee and the FDA to take this opportunity to adopt a better policy in the interest of American patients, physicians, and public health.

title: Comment from Doug Gaines
comment:
Subject: Public Comment Supporting Inclusion of BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon on the Section 503A Bulks List – Docket FDA-2025-N-6895

Dear Members of the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee and FDA Staff,

As a concerned citizen who has directly observed the real-world effects of these peptide therapies on individuals seeking improved health outcomes, I strongly support their inclusion. These compounds represent an important tool for personalized, patient-specific compounding that can address unmet needs in areas such as gastrointestinal health, wound healing, inflammation, metabolic function, sleep, and overall resilience.

Background
Inclusion on the 503A Bulks List would allow licensed compounding pharmacies, under a valid prescription and physician oversight, to prepare customized formulations when no suitable FDA-approved product meets a patient’s specific clinical needs.

Analysis
Excluding these substances would restrict access to therapies that many compounding pharmacies have prepared for years based on emerging science and clinical demand.

Preclinical research and available data provide a foundation of promise: BPC-157 has demonstrated potential in animal models for gut repair and tissue healing relevant to ulcerative colitis; KPV and TB-500 show anti-inflammatory and wound-healing properties; MOTS-c has been studied for its role in mitochondrial function and metabolic health, aligning with its evaluation for obesity; and the remaining peptides have data supporting roles in sleep regulation, stress response, and neuroprotection.

Beyond laboratory data, individuals I know and others in patient communities have reported substantial, tangible benefits from properly compounded versions of these peptides. These include meaningful weight loss and improved metabolic markers with MOTS-c, accelerated recovery from injuries and reduced inflammation with BPC-157, KPV, and TB-500, and better sleep quality plus overall vitality with Emideltide, Semax, and Epitalon. In an environment where many people face ongoing challenges from dietary, environmental, and lifestyle factors that contribute to inflammation, metabolic dysregulation, and reduced healing capacity, these therapies have helped some individuals achieve noticeable improvements in function, energy, and quality of life — often reducing their reliance on multiple conventional medications.

The agency’s current approach may undervalue the accumulated real-world experience from compounding use and the perspectives of patients and practitioners who have seen these substances perform in clinical settings. Patient-reported outcomes and practitioner observations constitute valuable evidence, especially for conditions where individualized dosing and formulations matter. Distributional impacts also favor inclusion: these therapies can benefit a broad range of patients, including those for whom approved options are unavailable, unsuitable, or prohibitively expensive.

Recommendations
1.Recommend inclusion of BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Emideltide (DSIP), Semax, and Epitalon on the Section 503A Bulks List for the specific uses evaluated by the agency.
2.Require that compounded products meet rigorous quality and sterility standards consistent with 503A requirements.
3.Implement targeted post-inclusion monitoring to continue building the safety and effectiveness database.
4.Encourage nominators and researchers to pursue additional clinical studies while allowing patient access in the interim under medical supervision.

Conclusion
Including these peptides on the 503A Bulks List would advance public health by expanding safe, regulated access to promising therapies that address real patient needs in healing, metabolic health, inflammation, sleep, and overall wellness. It would respect patient and practitioner experience, support innovation in compounding, and provide a controlled pathway forward rather than driving demand underground. title: Comment from Tommy Tuberville
comment:
Dear Chairperson:

Last July I wrote to Secretary Kennedy asking him to restore legal compounding access to peptide therapies that doctors and patients across Alabama had been cut off from. The FDA's April 2026 removal of these compounds from Category 2 was the right call. I am writing now to urge the Committee to follow through and recommend inclusion of the seven compounds scheduled for review on July 23 and 24 onto the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List. A favorable recommendation is the necessary next step toward establishing a legal compounding pathway for these therapies.

The 2023 Restrictions Were a Mistake
The Biden-era FDA applied a clinical trial standard designed for commercial drug manufacturers to compounding pharmacies that fill individual patient prescriptions under physician orders. That was the wrong test. None of these compounds were restricted because anyone proved they were dangerous. They were restricted because the review process was not built for what compounders actually do. The April 2026 reversal acknowledges that. The July hearings can be where it gets corrected.

The Gray Market Washington Created Is the Real Problem
When the FDA shut off regulated compounding access, patients did not stop using these therapies. They bought them from unregulated online vendors and foreign suppliers, many based in China, selling raw compounds with no testing, no quality controls, and no physician involvement. No prescription required. No USP standards. No accountability. Secretary Kennedy said it plainly: with the gray market, you have no idea what you are getting, and a lot of it is substandard. He is right. The 2023 restrictions did not make these therapies less available. They made them less safe.

A licensed U.S. compounding pharmacy operates under an entirely different standard: FDA-registered suppliers, sterility testing, potency verification, and a valid prescription from a physician who knows the patient. That infrastructure is what protects people. The Committee'srecommendation determines whether a legal pathway to that standard exists for these seven compounds.

Request
I am asking the Committee to recommend inclusion of all seven compounds on the 503A Bulk Drug Substances List — BPC-157, KPV , TB-500, MOTS-C, Emideltide/DSIP, Semax, and Epitalon — evaluated on their safety profiles and suitability for compounding, not on the absence of a commercial drug application. A favorable recommendation initiates the rulemaking process through which legal compounding access can be formally established. The federal government created this gray market by closing the regulated alternative. The July hearings are the opportunity to begin fixing that.

title: Comment from Enhanced Group Inc. (NYSE:ENHA)
comment:
Enhanced Group, Inc. (NYSE: ENHA) submits this comment in formal support of reclassifying BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTs-C, Emideltide, Semax, and Epitalon from Category 2 to Category 1 under FDA's bulk drug substance framework for compounding.

The current Category 2 classification has driven demand for these peptides into an unregulated gray market rather than suppressing it. Survey data show that roughly half of peptide users mistakenly believe these compounds are FDA-approved, and independent quality testing has found that close to a third of research-grade peptide products fail basic quality checks, with no lot tracking or adverse-event reporting. Reclassification would bring these compounds into licensed, physician-supervised channels where product integrity and patient safety can be assured.

Enhanced Group has firsthand experience with this regulatory gap: our IRB-approved athlete research program excluded these peptides specifically because no compliant sourcing pathway currently exists, despite their documented therapeutic potential. We have made a categorical commitment not to source peptide compounds from overseas bulk suppliers, and we believe reclassification is necessary to support that kind of domestic, compliant supply chain.

This comment is submitted with the endorsement of Enhanced's Independent Medical Commission, chaired by Prof. Dr. Dr. Guido Pieles and including Dr. Abud Al Bakri. Full details, data citations, and the Commission's endorsement are included in the attached formal letter.

Enhanced Group respectfully urges the Committee to vote in favor of reclassification.
